1.text: *Alif-Lãm-Mĩm.* Three letters, no verb, no sentence, and no meaning that any dictionary will give you. This is the first verse of the longest sūrah in the Qurʾān, and it is not a statement at all. Maʿārif-ul-Qurʾān explains the form before anything else. Several sūrahs open with a combination of Arabic letters — *Ḥā-Mīm*, *Alif-Lām-Mīm-Ṣād*, and so on. Each letter is pronounced on its own, without a vowel added after it, which is why the technical term for them is *muqaṭṭaʿāt*, isolated letters. Tazkīrul Qurʾān counts them: they appear at the beginning of twenty-nine chapters, and some of them became the names of the sūrahs themselves — *Ṭā-Hā*, *Yā-Sīn*, *Ṣād*, *Qāf*. **What the scholars said about them.** There are three positions, and it matters which one you hold. Some commentators took them to be the names of the sūrahs they head. Others took them to be symbols of the Divine Names. Tanwīr al-Miqbās preserves this line of reading from Ibn ʿAbbās in several forms: *Alif* stands for Allah, *Lām* for the angel Jibrīl, and *Mīm* for Muḥammad; or *Alif* stands for Allah's blessings, *Lām* for His kindness and *Mīm* for His dominion; or they are the opening letters of three of His Names — Allah, al-Laṭīf, al-Majīd. Some held it is an oath He has taken. The majority position is different, and Maʿārif is explicit that this is where most of the Companions, the Tābiʿūn and the later authoritative scholars landed: the isolated letters are symbols whose meaning is known to Allah alone, or was entrusted to the Prophet ﷺ as a confidence not to be passed on. The evidence for that reading is negative and strong — no explanation of these letters was ever reported from him. Al-Qurṭubī adopted this view. Al-Jalālayn states it in a single line: God knows best what He means by these letters. **Why they are there at all.** Al-Mukhtaṣar gives the functional answer. The letters have no meaning in themselves, but they have a purpose. Since there is divine wisdom in everything in the Qurʾān, these letters point to the miracle of a book made out of the same letters that make up ordinary human speech. And he adds an observation you can check: when a sūrah opens with letters like these, it is usually followed by a verse about the Qurʾān itself. That is exactly what happens here. The very next verse is *This is the Book.* So the letters are a challenge before the claim. Here are the components — the alphabet you already use — and here is what has been built from them. **What Ibn Kathīr does instead.** Worth knowing: Ibn Kathīr does not spend his entry on the letters. He opens with the merits of the sūrah itself, and the reports he gathers are worth having. In the Musnad of Aḥmad, Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, at-Tirmidhī and an-Nasāʾī, Abū Hurayrah reports that the Prophet ﷺ said: *Do not turn your houses into graves. Verily, Shayṭān does not enter the house where Sūrat al-Baqarah is recited.* At-Tirmidhī graded it ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ. Ibn Masʿūd said: *Shayṭān flees from the house where Sūrat al-Baqarah is heard.* An-Nasāʾī collected it in *al-Yawm wal-Laylah*, and al-Ḥākim in his *Mustadrak*, calling its chain authentic while noting that the two Ṣaḥīḥs did not carry it. Ad-Dārimī records from ash-Shaʿbī, from Ibn Masʿūd: *Whoever recites ten verses from Sūrat al-Baqarah in a night, Shayṭān will not enter his house that night; whoever recites it during a day in his house, Shayṭān will not enter that house for three days.* Abū al-Qāsim aṭ-Ṭabarānī, Ibn Ḥibbān in his Ṣaḥīḥ, and Ibn Marduwayh all carry it. Al-Bukhārī records Usayd ibn Ḥuḍayr reciting al-Baqarah at night with his horse tethered beside him, and something approaching that he could not make out. The Prophet ﷺ told him: *Those were the angels. They came close to hear your voice, and had you kept reading, people would have been able to see them when morning came.* A sūrah that opens with three unexplained letters, and whose opening report is about what happens in a room when it is read aloud.

2.text: *This is the Book! There is no doubt about it—a guide for those mindful ˹of Allah˺.* The verse makes a claim about itself, and then narrows who benefits from it. Both halves deserve attention. **Why "this" and not "that".** Maʿārif raises the difficulty directly. The Arabic reads *dhālika'l-kitāb*, and *dhālika* — *that* — is a pronoun used to point at something distant. But the Book being referred to is the Qurʾān, which is right here in front of the reader. The demonstrative seems wrong. Maʿārif's reading is that it is not wrong but deliberate. The pronoun points back to the prayer at the end of al-Fātiḥah — *Guide us along the Straight Path.* That request has now been answered, and this Book is the answer. The distance in the pronoun is the distance between asking and receiving. Al-Jalālayn reads the same feature differently: the demonstrative is there to glorify the Book. Both readings agree that the choice of word is doing work. **"There is no doubt about it".** Ibn Kathīr's entry is largely a roll call. As-Suddī reports that Abū Mālik and Abū Ṣāliḥ transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbās, and Murrah al-Hamadhānī from Ibn Masʿūd, along with several other Companions, that *in which there is no rayb* means *about which there is no doubt.* Abū ad-Dardāʾ, Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, Abū Mālik, Nāfiʿ, ʿAṭāʾ, Abū al-ʿĀliyah, ar-Rabīʿ ibn Anas, Muqātil ibn Ḥayyān, as-Suddī, Qatādah and Ismāʿīl ibn Abī Khālid all said the same. Then Ibn Kathīr records Ibn Abī Ḥātim: *I do not know of any disagreement over this explanation.* For a word as loaded as this one, that is unusual. Some scholars read the sentence as carrying a prohibition rather than a description — *do not doubt the Qurʾān.* **Where to pause when reciting.** Ibn Kathīr notes a live disagreement among the reciters. Some pause after *there is no doubt* and then continue *in which there is guidance for those mindful of Allah.* He judges it better to pause after *in which there is no doubt*, because on that reading *guidance* becomes an attribute of the Book itself rather than merely something contained in it — and that carries the stronger meaning. It is a small point about breath, and it changes what the verse asserts. **Who the mindful are.** Ibn ʿAbbās is recorded twice on *al-muttaqīn*. First: *the believers who avoid associating partners with Allah and who work in His obedience.* Second: *those who fear Allah's punishment, which would result if they abandoned the guidance they recognise and know, and who hope in Allah's mercy by believing in what He revealed.* Fear and hope, again, as in 1:5. Qatādah simply points forward: *al-muttaqīn* are the people Allah describes in the next verse — *who believe in the unseen and establish prayer.* Ibn ʿAbbās and Ibn Masʿūd render the phrase as *a light for those who have taqwā.* **Why only they.** This is the part most easily misread. The verse does not say the Book is unclear and only the pious can decode it. Tazkīrul Qurʾān explains the mechanism: there is no doubt that the Qurʾān is a book of guidance, but it guides only those who are sincere in searching for truth and anxious to be guided. The search is already in human nature; what is required is to uncover it. Al-Mukhtaṣar puts the claim and the condition together: this is the Qurʾān, in which there is nothing of any doubt, neither in its origin nor in its meaning — and it guides those who are mindful of Allah to the way that leads to Him. Tanwīr al-Miqbās adds a harder edge, offering among its readings that there is no doubt it has come from God: believe in it and be guided, or do not, and face the consequence. And one of its readings ties the verse to the earlier scriptures — that there is no doubt the description and traits of Muḥammad ﷺ are to be found in the Torah and the Gospel, which the next verse then takes up.

3.text: *Who believe in the unseen, establish prayer, and donate from what We have provided for them.* Three clauses, and they are not a list of duties so much as a map of where belief shows up: in what you accept, in what you do with your body, and in what you do with your money. **What faith means.** Ibn Kathīr opens on the word itself and lets the early authorities disagree. Abū Jaʿfar ar-Rāzī transmits through al-ʿAlāʾ ibn al-Musayyib ibn Rāfiʿ, from Abū Isḥāq, from Abū al-Aḥwaṣ, from ʿAbdullāh: *Īmān is to trust.* ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥah reports from Ibn ʿAbbās that *who have faith* means *they trust.* Maʿmar reports from az-Zuhrī: *Īmān is deeds.* Abū Jaʿfar ar-Rāzī reports from ar-Rabīʿ ibn Anas: *they have faith* means *they fear Allah.* Four definitions from four authorities, and Ibn Kathīr does not simply pick one. He notes that linguistically, in the absolute sense, *īmān* means trust, and the Qurʾān uses it that way — *he trusts in Allah and trusts in the believers* (9:61), and Yūsuf's brothers saying *you will never believe us even when we speak the truth* (12:17). Some scholars explained *īmān* as *khashyah*, fear of Allah. Then he gives Ibn Jarīr's synthesis, which is the one worth keeping: the preferred view is that they are described as having faith in the unseen by tongue, deed and creed together. *Īmān* is a general term covering affirmation of Allah, His Books and His Messengers, and then realising that affirmation by acting on what the tongue has said. Belief, affirmation and action are not three candidates for the meaning. They are one thing described from three sides. **What the unseen is.** Ibn Kathīr says plainly that the Salaf differed on this and that all their explanations are correct, pointing at the same general meaning. Abū Jaʿfar ar-Rāzī quotes ar-Rabīʿ ibn Anas reporting from Abū al-ʿĀliyah: *They believe in Allah, His angels, His Books, His Messengers, the Last Day, His Paradise, His Fire, and in the meeting with Him. All of this is the unseen.* Qatādah ibn Diʿāmah said the same. Tanwīr al-Miqbās lists more concretely: that which is hidden from them, such as Paradise, Hell, the Bridge, the Scale, the Resurrection and the Reckoning. It records two further readings — that they believe in the unseen revealed in the Qurʾān as well as in what is not revealed in it, and that the unseen referred to is Allah Himself. Al-Jalālayn is shortest: what is hidden from them of the Resurrection, Paradise and the Fire. **Establishing prayer, not merely performing it.** The translation says *establish*, and the Arabic is stronger than *perform.* Tanwīr al-Miqbās unpacks it: they complete the five prescribed prayers, including the ablution that precedes them, the bowing and the prostrations, and what is obligatory in them with respect to their appointed times. Al-Jalālayn compresses the same idea: they perform it giving it its due. Establishing a prayer means it is built into the structure of the day rather than fitted around it. **Spending from what was given.** Note the framing in the verse itself: *from what We have provided for them.* Ownership is already qualified before the spending is mentioned. Tanwīr al-Miqbās reads it as giving charity from the wealth Allah gave them, and records the narrower reading that it means the obligatory poor-due, zakāh. Al-Jalālayn: they expend in obedience to God. **How the three clauses connect.** Tazkīrul Qurʾān offers the most coherent account of why these three belong together, tracing each back to an instinct that precedes it. True searching and true finding are the early and later stages of a single journey; whoever searches for truth unlocks faculties in himself that were closed. The vague yearnings of human nature then begin to receive a definite response, and that awakening is an attempt to discern the world of meanings behind the world of forms. When that leads to a discovery, it becomes faith in the unseen. What began as an urge to submit to some higher power takes the form of bowing to the Almighty. What began as a wish to sacrifice oneself for a greater good takes the form of spending one's wealth in God's cause. The verse is not listing requirements. It is describing what one inward movement looks like once it has become three outward habits.

4.text: *And who believe in what has been revealed to you ˹O Prophet˺ and what was revealed before you, and have sure faith in the Hereafter.* The previous verse described belief in the unseen generally. This one names its two objects — revelation, including revelation that came before this Book — and then adds a word the previous verse did not use. **No distinction between the messengers.** Ibn ʿAbbās's explanation, recorded by Ibn Kathīr, is direct: *They believe in what Allah sent you with, and in what the previous messengers were sent with. They do not distinguish between them, nor do they reject what they brought from their Lord.* Al-Mukhtaṣar states the same with the phrase that carries the weight: they believe in what Allah sent down to you, O Prophet, and in what He revealed to all the other prophets before you, *without distinction.* That clause excludes a specific failure — accepting some prophets and discarding others — which is precisely the charge the Qurʾān will press later in this sūrah. **Who this verse is about.** Maʿārif preserves a report from the Companions ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd and ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAbbās that gives the verse a historical setting. In the Prophet's lifetime, the God-fearing were of two kinds: those who had been polytheists and disbelievers and then accepted Islam, and those who had been People of the Book and embraced Islam later. The preceding verse describes the first group; this verse describes the second. That is why belief in the earlier Books is mentioned here specifically. According to the ḥadīth Maʿārif cites, the second group earns a double reward — first for believing in and following the earlier Books before the Qurʾān came to supersede them, and second for believing in and following the Qurʾān when it arrived as the final Book. Maʿārif adds the standing obligation: it remains obligatory for every Muslim to believe in the earlier divine Books. **Ibn Kathīr's structural note.** He records Mujāhid's mapping of the whole opening: *Four verses at the beginning of Sūrat al-Baqarah describe the believers, two describe the disbelievers, and thirteen describe the hypocrites.* Four, two, thirteen. The sūrah's opening is not a preamble; it is a table of contents for the human types it will spend its length on. Ibn Kathīr then widens the scope of the four verses: they are general and include every believer — Arab or non-Arab, a person of a previous scripture or not, jinn or human. And he draws an inference worth noting: if believers among the People of the Book gain two rewards, other Muslims whose faith is firmer may gain a reward equal to those two. **The word that changes: certainty.** The verse ends *and in the Hereafter they are certain* — and *certain* is a stronger word than *believe.* Al-Jalālayn's rendering shows the difference is not decorative. Ibn Kathīr lists what that certainty covers: the resurrection, the standing on the Day of Resurrection, Paradise, the Fire, the reckoning and the Scale that weighs deeds, the mīzān. Al-Mukhtaṣar: a definite belief in the Afterlife, with its rewards and punishments. So the two verses run: belief in the unseen, then certainty about the unseen. The first is acceptance of what cannot be verified; the second is that acceptance having settled into conviction. The believers described here have already made that crossing, which is why the very next verse announces they are guided — not that they are trying.

5.text: *It is they who are ˹truly˺ guided by their Lord, and it is they who will be successful.* Four verses have described a type of person. This one closes the description, and it is deliberately short — fifty-six words in the plan where the verses around it run to nine hundred. Brevity is the point. After four verses of qualification, the verdict needs no elaboration. **Note what the verse does not say.** It does not say they will be guided. It says they *are* upon guidance. The Arabic construction — *ulāʾika ʿalā hudā* — puts them already standing on it, not moving towards it. Guidance is not the reward promised at the end; it is the condition they are in. Ibn Kathīr's entry is the shortest of the seven and stays close to the text: *On guidance* means they are following a light, guidance and insight from Allah; *and they are the successful* means in this world and the Hereafter. **"Upon" guidance, not "in" it.** Tanwīr al-Miqbās expands the preposition: these people, who have these traits, are on guidance from their Lord — they enjoy favour, mercy and clear exposition that has come down from Him. It adds a second reading: the successful are those who have grasped and found what they were seeking, and have escaped the evil of what they were fleeing. That pairing is the shape of the whole promise. Success here is defined twice, once as attainment and once as escape. Al-Jalālayn gives the same two halves in the plainest terms: those described in this way are upon guidance from their Lord, and they are the ones who will prosper — meaning they will succeed in entering Paradise and be saved from the Fire. Maʿārif compresses it to a single sentence: those who possess these qualities are on the path of guidance and will be successful in this world and the next, gaining what they desire and being saved from what they fear. **Why the demonstrative is repeated.** *It is they* … *and it is they.* The Arabic repeats *ulāʾika*, and the repetition restricts the claim in the same way the fronted object did in 1:5. It is not guidance in general that is being described, and not success in general. It is these people, and they specifically. That restriction is what makes the next verse land. The sūrah has just said who succeeds; the very next verse turns to those for whom warning and non-warning have become identical, and the contrast is the argument. **Where the first unit ends.** Mujāhid's count, recorded by Ibn Kathīr at 2:4, put four verses to the believers. This is the fourth — the conclusion rather than a fifth quality. The description is complete: belief in the unseen, prayer, spending, belief in all revelation, certainty about the Hereafter. Then the verdict. Tanwīr al-Miqbās records a reading that identifies the group historically rather than typologically: these are the Companions of Muḥammad ﷺ. The verse was revealed among people who could see the description being lived out beside them, which is why it needed no explanation when it first arrived.

6.text: *As for those who persist in disbelief, it is the same whether you warn them or not—they will never believe.* The sūrah turns abruptly. Four verses on the guided, and now two on those for whom guidance has stopped being available. The shift is the argument: the same Book produces opposite results in different people, and verse two already told you why. **What disbelief means here.** Ibn Kathīr gives the root sense first: *those who disbelieve* means those who covered the truth and hid it. The word is not about absence of conviction. It is about something present being concealed. That matters for reading the rest of the verse. These are not people who have never encountered the claim. They are people who have, and have covered it over. **The Prophet's own reluctance.** Ibn Kathīr records through ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥah, from Ibn ʿAbbās, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was eager for all people to believe and to follow the guidance he had been sent with. That report explains the verse's tone. The statement that warning makes no difference is not delivered coldly. It is addressed to a man who wanted the opposite and kept warning anyway, and it exists to release him from an expectation he could not meet. Al-Jalālayn draws the practical conclusion bluntly: it is alike to them whether you have warned them or not, they do not believe, *as God knows very well — so do not hope that they will believe.* Al-Jalālayn names examples: the likes of Abū Jahl and Abū Lahab. It also records a grammatical note on the recitation of *a-andhartahum*, whether both hamzas are pronounced or the second is softened into an alif, with or without an inserted alif between them. And it defines the word itself: *indhār*, warning, is to give knowledge of something while simultaneously instilling an element of fear. Warning is not neutral information. It is information delivered with its consequences attached. **Stubbornness, not ignorance.** Al-Mukhtaṣar's reading is short and specific: those who reject what Allah revealed to His Messenger continue on the wrong path *in their stubbornness*. So it makes no difference whether you warn them or not. Tanwīr al-Miqbās makes the same point about volition: whether you instil fear in them by means of the Qurʾān or you do not, it is all one for them — they do not *want* to believe. It adds a second reading, that they will not believe because it stands in Allah's knowledge. **Why Maʿārif places this verse here.** Maʿārif's account of the sūrah's structure is the clearest available. Having affirmed the Qurʾān as the Book of guidance beyond all doubt, the first five verses describe those who benefit from it fully — the *muʾminūn* or *muttaqūn* — and set out the qualities that distinguish them. The next fifteen verses describe those who refuse this guidance and oppose it out of spite and blind malice. And in the Prophet's time there were two distinct groups of them. One came out into open hostility and rejection, and the Qurʾān calls them *kāfirūn*. The other, out of moral weakness and greed, did not have the courage to say what they thought, and took the route of deceit and duplicity — telling the Muslims they believed, while working against them. Two verses for the first group, thirteen for the second. The hypocrites get more than six times the attention, which tells you where the sūrah thinks the real danger lies. **Why truth is refused.** Tazkīrul Qurʾān gives the social mechanism, and it is the most uncomfortable part of this verse. However clear the call of truth may be, it can only be understood and accepted by a mind that is open to it. God's inaudible call in the universe, and the preacher's audible expression of it, cannot touch closed minds. Then the harder observation: where a society is rigidly bound by age-old convention, people are less concerned with opening their minds to divine realities than with protecting the vested interests of the existing system. The preacher, as God's emissary, is neither a representative nor a supporter of that structure. His call is new and unfamiliar, and it presents itself as a threat to material security. On that reading, verse six is not describing a theological failure. It is describing what happens when truth arrives in a place where people have something to lose.

7.text: *Allah has sealed their hearts and their hearing, and their sight is covered. They will suffer a tremendous punishment.* Verse six said warning makes no difference. This verse says why — and the explanation is the difficult part, because the sealing is attributed to Allah. **What the sealing is.** Ibn Kathīr gathers the early explanations and they converge on a process rather than an arbitrary act. As-Suddī: *khatama Allāh* means *Allah has sealed.* Qatādah gives the sequence: *Shayṭān gained control of them when they obeyed him; therefore Allah sealed their hearts, their hearing and their sight, and they could neither see the guidance nor hear it, comprehend it or understand it.* Obedience first, sealing after. Ibn Jurayj reports from Mujāhid: *A stamp. It occurs when sin resides in the heart and surrounds it from all sides, and this submersion of the heart in sin constitutes a stamp — meaning a seal.* Mujāhid also ranked the stages, through ʿAbdullāh ibn Kathīr: *the stain is not as bad as the stamp, and the stamp is not as bad as the lock, which is the worst type.* Al-Aʿmash describes Mujāhid demonstrating it with his hand — the heart held open like a palm, then closed. And Mujāhid connected it to the *rān* of 83:14, the covering that grows over a heart. None of these describe a verdict handed down from nowhere. They describe a heart that has been progressively closed by its own choices until the closing is complete. **The consensus, and the prayer that answers it.** Al-Qurṭubī's statement, quoted by Ibn Kathīr, settles the doctrine: the ummah has agreed that Allah has described Himself as sealing and closing the hearts of the disbelievers *as a punishment for their disbelief.* He cites the parallel verse — *Nay, Allah has set a seal upon their hearts because of their disbelief* (4:155) — where the cause is stated explicitly. Al-Qurṭubī then does something telling. He immediately cites the Prophet's supplication, *O You who changes the hearts, make our hearts firm upon Your religion*, and the ḥadīth of Ḥudhayfah in the Ṣaḥīḥ: *Trials are presented to the hearts as the straws of a woven mat are laid one after another…* ending with a heart that no longer recognises what is right or refuses what is wrong. The sealing is real, and it is also reversible enough to be prayed against. That is why the Prophet ﷺ prayed it. **How the punishment works in this life.** Maʿārif's contribution is the most searching. These verses tell us that the Hereafter is where the real punishment for disbelief is received — but some punishment arrives in this world, and it can take a graver form than pain. The divine favour that enables a person to reform himself is withdrawn. Then, with no thought for how the deeds will be assessed on the Day of Judgment, he keeps growing in disobedience until he loses even the awareness that what he is doing is evil. Maʿārif quotes the elders: one punishment for an evil deed is the evil deed that follows it, and one reward for a good deed is the good deed that follows it. He then cites the ḥadīth of the black dot. When a man commits a sin, a black dot appears on his heart, and that first dot disturbs him the way a smudge on white cloth always does. But if instead of seeking pardon he commits a second, another dot appears — and so with every new sin, until the covering is complete. That is verse seven from the inside. The seal is not applied at once. It is built. **What the three faculties mean.** The verse names three, and they are not redundant. Al-Mukhtaṣar separates them cleanly: Allah has sealed their hearts, locking their falsehood inside; He has sealed their hearing, so that they neither listen to nor accept the truth; and He has placed a cover over their eyes, so that they do not see the truth in its clarity. Al-Jalālayn gives each its function: a seal on the hearts, impressing on them and making certain that no good enters; something deposited in the hearing so they cannot profit from the truth they hear; a veil over the eyes so they do not see it. Affection, attention and perception — the three ways a person takes truth in, all closed. **Who it was about, and what comes next.** Tanwīr al-Miqbās records two identifications: particular Jews of Madīnah — Kaʿb ibn al-Ashraf, Ḥuyayy ibn Akhṭab and Judayy ibn Akhṭab — or the idolaters of Makkah, ʿUtbah ibn Rabīʿah, Shaybah ibn Rabīʿah and al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīrah. Al-Mukhtaṣar closes by turning the page, and his note is the hinge into the next thirteen verses: after describing the disbelievers, who are at fault inside and out, Allah describes the hypocrites, who appear good on the outside and are not so within. The sūrah has now sorted people into the guided and the sealed. The third group — the ones who look like the first and are the second — is what it spends the next thirteen verses on.

8.text: *And there are some who say, "We believe in Allah and the Last Day," yet they are not ˹true˺ believers.* Two verses described the guided, two described those who openly refuse. Now a third group appears, and it is the one the sūrah spends the most space on — thirteen verses here against two for the open disbelievers. **What hypocrisy is.** Ibn Kathīr opens with the definition: *nifāq* means to show conformity or agreement and to conceal evil. Then he gives the history, and it explains why this group appears here rather than in the Makkan sūrahs. In the early period in Madīnah there were no hypocrites at all, because the Muslims were not yet strong enough to be worth pretending for. Only a few Jews embraced Islam, such as ʿAbdullāh ibn Salām. Then came Badr. ʿAbdullāh ibn Ubayy ibn Salūl — a leader in Madīnah — said *Allah's religion has become apparent*, and pretended to be Muslim, along with many like him and many among the People of the Book. Hypocrisy, in other words, is what unbelief becomes when unbelief stops paying. It is not a doctrine. It is a calculation. Ibn Kathīr sets the cost of the alternative beside it: a Muslim emigrating from Makkah had to abandon his wealth, his children and his land, seeking Allah's reward in the Hereafter. The hypocrite keeps all three and adds a declaration. **Who they were.** Muḥammad ibn Isḥāq narrates that Ibn ʿAbbās said this verse refers to *the hypocrites among the Aws and Khazraj, and those who behaved as they did.* Abū al-ʿĀliyah, al-Ḥasan, Qatādah and as-Suddī explained it the same way. Al-Jalālayn records the same and adds why the verse names two beliefs rather than three: *the Last Day* is the Day of Resurrection *because it is the very last day.* **What they left out.** Maʿārif makes an observation that is easy to read past. Look at what they actually claimed: faith in Allah and in the Last Day. They did not claim faith in the Prophet ﷺ. Maʿārif's reading is that this was deliberate, and that it says something about lying itself. Even the hypocrites, with all their hostility to Islam, tried to keep clear of an outright lie as far as they could. In claiming to be Muslims they mentioned only belief in Allah and the Day of Judgment, and omitted belief in the Prophet ﷺ *for fear of telling a lie.* They were willing to deceive. They were not quite willing to be liars. The verse records the distinction without letting them keep it — because a claim designed to omit the one thing that would make it false is still a claim. **The tongue alone.** Ibn Kathīr is blunt about the mechanism: they utter these false statements only with their tongues. He cites the parallel in 63:1 — *When the hypocrites come to you, they say, "We bear witness that you are indeed the Messenger of Allah." Allah knows that you are indeed His Messenger.* They say the true sentence; they do not mean it. Ibn Abī Ḥātim records Ibn Jurayj on the same behaviour, and his account is the practical one: *the hypocrites pronounce "there is no deity worthy of worship except Allah" seeking to ensure the sanctity of their blood and their money, all the while concealing disbelief.* That is the whole transaction. The declaration is not a belief. It is an insurance policy. Tanwīr al-Miqbās parses it accordingly: *We believe in Allah* — in the open, and we are genuine; *and the Last Day* — we believe in resurrection after death, when deeds are requited; *yet they do not believe* — that is, not inwardly, and not genuinely. Tazkīrul Qurʾān supplies the psychology. For those who put worldly interest and expediency first, total and unconditional devotion to truth looks unwise, because their real allegiance is to their interests and they can only attach themselves to truth superficially. They consider themselves clever.

9.text: *They seek to deceive Allah and the believers, yet they only deceive themselves, but they fail to perceive it.* The verse contains an impossibility and then resolves it. You cannot deceive Allah. So what is the sentence doing? **Why Allah is named at all.** Maʿārif addresses this head-on and his answer is the key to the verse. These verses denounce the hypocrites for trying to be clever with Allah Himself — *although no one among them could probably have had such an intention, or even thought of such a possibility.* What they were actually doing was trying to deceive the Prophet ﷺ and the Muslims. Allah has equated that with an attempt to deceive Him, and thereby established a principle: whoever is impertinent to a prophet or to a man of Allah is ultimately guilty of being impertinent to Allah Himself — above all in the case of the Prophet ﷺ, who stands at the head of all created beings. Al-Jalālayn makes the same point as a note on rhetoric: the mention of *God* in this statement is for rhetorical effect. He is not described as being deceived. He is named so that deceiving His Messenger is seen for what it is. **The grammar of a one-way action.** Al-Jalālayn then does something the English cannot. The verb *yukhādiʿūn* is the third form, which normally implies reciprocity — mutual deceiving. But here, he notes, it denotes a one-way action, and he gives the classical illustration: *ʿāqabtu al-lissa*, *I punished the thief*, uses the third form *ʿāqaba* even though the thief is not punishing back. So the reciprocal form is doing ironic work. The verse uses the shape of a two-way transaction to describe something that was only ever one-way. He also records a variant reading: *wa-mā yakhdaʿūna* in place of *wa-mā yukhādiʿūna*. **Who is actually being deceived.** Al-Jalālayn's answer: they deceive God and the believers by manifesting the opposite of the unbelief they hide, so that they can avoid His rulings in this world — *and only themselves they deceive*, because the consequences rebound on them. They are disgraced in this world when God makes known to His Prophet what they are hiding, and they are punished in the Hereafter. Al-Mukhtaṣar states it plainly: they think they can deceive Allah and the believers by acting outside as if they believe while hiding disbelief inside, but really they only deceive themselves without realising it. Allah knows all that is secret and hidden, and has told the believers what these people are like. That last clause is the sting. The deception failed not only in God's knowledge but in published fact — the sūrah being recited is itself the exposure. **And they do not notice.** Both halves of the verse end in non-perception. Tanwīr al-Miqbās gives the reason: they do not know that Allah informs His Prophet of what lies secret in their hearts. It also records the harsher reading of the opening — that they were so daring with Allah that they thought they had actually deceived Him. It identifies *the believers* concretely as Abū Bakr and all the Companions of Muḥammad ﷺ. Ibn Jurayj, via Ibn Abī Ḥātim, gives the motive once more: they pronounced the declaration *seeking to ensure the sanctity of their blood and their money.* The transaction was never about belief. It was about assets — and the verse says the only asset they actually moved was their own position.

10.text:
*There is sickness in their hearts, and Allah ˹only˺ lets their sickness increase. They will suffer a painful punishment for their lies.* The previous verse said they do not perceive. This one explains why — and the explanation is medical. **What the Qurʾān means by disease.** Maʿārif gives the fullest account in the corpus and it is worth following carefully, because the metaphor is doing precise work. Illness in the ordinary medical sense, he writes, is a state in which a person has lost the balanced proportion of the elements within him that keep him healthy, so that his body can no longer function properly — which may finally lead to his total destruction. In the terminology of the Qurʾān and the ḥadīth, the same word is applied to certain mental or psychic states which prevent a person from attaining any degree of spiritual perfection. They gradually deprive him of the ability to perform good deeds, and even of ordinary human decency, until he meets his spiritual death. Then Maʿārif quotes the great spiritual master Junayd of Baghdād: just as the diseases of the body arise from an imbalance among the four humours, the diseases of the heart arise from surrender to one's physical desires. According to this verse, the disease hidden in their hearts is unbelief and rejection of the truth — which is as much a real sickness as a physical one. The metaphor is exact, not decorative. A disease is not an intrusion from outside; it is the system's own balance lost. And a disease progresses. **Why the sickness increases.** The verse says Allah increases it, and the mechanism is the difficult part. Al-Jalālayn gives the sharpest version: God has increased their sickness *with what He has revealed in the Qurʾān, since they disbelieve it.* Revelation is the medicine. For a heart that rejects it, each new revelation is another thing rejected, and the rejection compounds. The cure is what makes them worse — not because it is harmful but because of what they do with it. Al-Mukhtaṣar describes the same process in the language of return: Allah increases the disease in their hearts and they reap what they sow. Because they lied, Allah increases the disease of doubt, adding hesitation to their uncertainty — *hence they only gain what they deserve.* Tanwīr al-Miqbās lists the contents of the disease: doubt, hypocrisy, conflict and darkness. And it identifies the individuals — the hypocrites ʿAbdullāh ibn Ubayy, Jadd ibn Qays and Muʿaṭṭib ibn Qushayr. **Two readings of the final word.** Al-Jalālayn records both. Read *yukadhdhibūn*, it means they used to call the Prophet of God a liar. Read *yakdhibūn*, it refers to their mendacity when they said *we believe.* The difference matters. One reading makes the crime rejection of the messenger; the other makes it the false declaration itself. The verse is describing people guilty of both, and the two readings cover each. **The punishment matches the organ.** Tanwīr al-Miqbās notes that the painful torment in the Hereafter *shall extend to their hearts.* The disease was in the heart; the punishment reaches the same place. Al-Mukhtaṣar adds the scope of the lie: they will have painful suffering because they lied against Allah and against the people, and rejected the message brought by Muḥammad ﷺ. **Why the increase is attributed to Allah.**

The verse says *Allah lets their sickness increase*, and that phrasing needs care, because it can be read as though Allah manufactures the disbelief and then punishes it.

The sources read it the other way round, and the difference is the whole verse. Al-Jalālayn ties the increase to the revelation itself: God has increased their sickness *with what He has revealed in the Qurʾān, since they disbelieve it.* The revelation is not the disease. It is what exposes the disease, and every exposure that is refused leaves the condition worse than it found it.

Al-Mukhtaṣar's phrasing keeps the agency where it belongs: *they reap what they sow.* Because they lied, Allah increases the disease of doubt in their hearts, adding hesitation to their uncertainty — hence they only gain what they deserve.

That is the same logic verse seven used of the sealed hearts, and the one Maʿārif drew out there: one punishment for an evil deed is the evil deed that follows it. The sequence across this opening is consistent. The open disbelievers were sealed; the hypocrites are diseased. Both conditions are built, not imposed.

**The contrast the sūrah is preparing.**

The disease is located in the heart, and earlier in this same opening the sūrah described another group by what is in theirs — light, and guidance from their Lord. The believers of 2:5 are *upon* guidance. These are *in* sickness.

That contrast is why the metaphor is medical rather than judicial. A verdict is delivered once. A disease is lived with, it progresses, and it can in principle be treated — which is part of why the sūrah describes this group at such length instead of dismissing it in two verses as it did the open disbelievers. Thirteen verses is not the space you give to people beyond reach.

Junayd's comparison makes the same point from the other side. Bodily disease comes from the humours losing their proportion; disease of the heart comes from surrender to one's desires. Neither is an invasion from outside. Both are what happens when an internal balance is given up — and in both cases the person inside is the one who must want it restored.

**Why this verse sits third.** Maʿārif's structural note is the reason the order matters: this verse *indicates why the hypocrites behave so foolishly and why they fail to see the folly of their course.* Verses eight and nine described the behaviour and its futility. Verse ten supplies the diagnosis. A person who cannot see that his cleverness is self-defeating is not making an error he could be argued out of; he has a condition. And the next two verses show what that condition sounds like from the outside — being told not to spread corruption, and answering that they are only peace-makers.

11.text: *When they are told, "Do not spread corruption in the land," they reply, "We are only peace-makers!"* The verse is a piece of reported speech on both sides, and the reply is the point. **What they were told.** Al-Jalālayn identifies the corruption specifically: *do not spread corruption in the land* — through unbelief, and by hindering people from faith. Al-Mukhtaṣar widens it: through their rejection of the truth, their disobedience, and so on. Tanwīr al-Miqbās reads the addressees as the Jews, and the mischief as *preventing people from the religion of Muḥammad* ﷺ, with their reply meaning *we are reforming it through obedience.* **The grammar of the reply.** Maʿārif makes the observation that carries the verse. Their answer is *innamā naḥnu muṣliḥūn*, and the word *innamā* indicates **not merely emphasis but exclusivity.** So they did not say *we are reformers too*, or *we mean well.* They said we are *nothing but* reformers — servants of order, whose activities could have nothing to do with disorder at all. That is a much stronger claim than a defence. It denies the category. **Why the claim fails.** Maʿārif's rebuttal is one sentence and it is the verse's real argument: oral claims alone do not decide whether a person is working for order or disorder, *for what thief would call himself a thief?* It depends on what one does, not on what one says. If a man's activities result in mischief, he will be called a mischief-maker even if he had no such intention. That last clause is important and is easy to miss. Maʿārif is not saying the hypocrites secretly intended corruption and lied about it. He is saying intention is not what makes an act corruptive — the outcome is. A person can be genuinely convinced of his own good faith and still be the source of the damage. Tazkīrul Qurʾān supplies the reasoning from inside their position. The hypocrites call their own policy one of reform; they prize it because it lets them pursue a safe course without clashing with anyone. And that, Tazkīrul says, is precisely what shows how distorted their reasoning has become — because on earth, reform can only come from a person giving himself up to God alone, and obstructing any movement that consolidates man's relationship with his Lord *is* creating disorder on earth. Their supposedly profitable business is running at a loss. They are trading pure truth for an adulterated version. **Why the sūrah reports the speech at all.** Quoting the reply rather than merely describing it does something description could not. The reader hears the tone — the confidence, the slight indignation at being accused. Verse ten said their hearts are diseased and that they cannot perceive it. Verse eleven lets you hear what that sounds like.

12.text: *Indeed, it is they who are the corruptors, but they fail to perceive it.* Fourteen words in English, and the verse is a flat contradiction of the one before it. They said *we are only peace-makers.* The answer is: no — and you cannot see that you are not. **The emphatic particle.** Al-Jalālayn notes that *alā* at the start is for alerting, and is intended emphatically. The verse does not simply assert the opposite of their claim; it calls attention before doing so. **Two levels of non-perception.** Tanwīr al-Miqbās separates them: they are indeed the mischief-mongers, by being a hindrance — *but they perceive not*, meaning the followers do not know that their leaders mislead them. That is a second blindness on top of the first. The leaders cannot see that they are corruptive, and the followers cannot see that they are being misled. The verse is short because the whole structure of the group is being described in one clause. Al-Mukhtaṣar puts both halves together: the truth is that it is they who ruin things, but they do not admit this, nor do they know that their actions are the cause of all ruin. **Why the sūrah needed this verse at all.** Verse eleven already reported the claim. Verse twelve exists to refuse it in God's own voice rather than by argument. That matters given what came before. Verse ten said their hearts carry a disease and that Allah increases it. If corruption were something they could be reasoned out of, the disease metaphor would be wrong — you argue with a mistake, you treat a condition. The verse therefore does not argue. It states, and then repeats the diagnosis: *but they fail to perceive it.* Maʿārif draws the general principle from the pair, and it is the one worth keeping beyond this sūrah: what a person calls himself decides nothing. What his activities produce decides everything. Tazkīrul Qurʾān's account of the same people is that every test in life moves them further from true religion and closer to their own world-oriented version of it. Their hypocrisy, in its phrase, is like a cancer which keeps growing.

13.text: *And when they are told, "Believe as others believe," they reply, "Will we believe as the fools believe?" Indeed, it is they who are fools, but they do not know.* The second exchange. The first was about what they do; this one is about what they think of the people who do it. **Who "others" are.** Maʿārif records the consensus of the commentators: the word *an-nās*, *the people*, in this verse refers to the blessed Companions of the Prophet ﷺ — because it was precisely these people who had embraced the faith and accepted the Qurʾān as the word of Allah while it was still being revealed. He draws the consequence, and it is a large one: the verse indicates that the only kind of faith acceptable to Allah is one similar to that of the Companions, and that the faith of anyone else deserves the name only insofar as it believes the same things in the same way. Ibn Kathīr gives the same reading with its chain: *believe as the people believe* means believe just as the believers believe — in Allah, His angels, His Books, His Messengers, resurrection after death, Paradise and the Fire. This is the tafsīr given by Abū al-ʿĀliyah and by as-Suddī in his tafsīr, with a chain of narration to Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn Masʿūd and other Companions. Tanwīr al-Miqbās names them individually: *as the people believe* means as ʿAbdullāh ibn Salām and his companions believed. Al-Jalālayn simply says: as the Companions of the Prophet. **What the reply reveals.** They do not dispute the content. They disparage the believers. Al-Mukhtaṣar catches the tone exactly: they reply *looking down on people and making fun of them.* Al-Jalālayn renders the refusal as a decision about company rather than about truth: *shall we believe as fools believe? That is, as the ignorant do? No — we do not follow their way.* That is the whole error in one sentence. The question they asked was not *is it true* but *who else believes it*, and having answered the second question they treated the first as settled. **The reversal.** *Indeed, it is they who are fools, but they do not know.* Ibn Kathīr adds a lexical point that sharpens the word. According to the majority of scholars, Allah uses the term *foolish* to include children — as in 4:5, *and do not give your property, which Allah has made a means of support for you, to the foolish.* So *sufahāʾ* is not primarily an insult about intelligence. It marks someone not yet competent to handle what has been entrusted to them. Applied here, it says the hypocrites have been given something they cannot manage — and their contempt for the believers is the symptom, not the argument. **Why they do not know.** Al-Mukhtaṣar: in fact it is they who are the fools, *but they are unaware of this.* Tanwīr al-Miqbās: *but they know not* that they are so. This is the third verse in a row ending in non-perception — 2:9 *they fail to perceive it*, 2:12 *they fail to perceive it*, 2:13 *they do not know*. The repetition is the point. Verse ten diagnosed a disease that increases. These three verses are what that disease looks like from outside: a person who cannot see his own deception, cannot see his own corruption, and cannot see his own foolishness. The sūrah has now given the group's two characteristic speeches. The next verse goes behind both, to what they say when the believers are not in the room.

14.text:
*When they meet the believers they say, "We believe." But when alone with their evil associates they say, "We are definitely with you; we were only mocking."* The two previous verses reported what the hypocrites said in public. This one reports the private conversation, and it is the verse the whole section has been building towards. **Two rooms.** Al-Mukhtaṣar sets out the calculation: when the hypocrites meet the believers they say *we believe what you believe*, because they think it will benefit them to act this way. But when they are alone with their leaders they say, *we are really with you and follow you — we are only making fun of them when we say that we believe.* Nothing is hidden here. The verse simply places the two statements side by side and lets the reader hold both. **Who their associates are.** Ibn Kathīr explains *shayāṭīnihim* — their devils — as their leaders and masters among the rabbis of the Jews, the hypocrites and the idolaters. Tanwīr al-Miqbās is more specific and names five: Kaʿb ibn al-Ashraf in Madīnah, Abū Burdah al-Aslamī in Banū Aslam, Ibn al-Sawdāʾ in al-Shām, ʿAbd al-Dār in Juhaynah, and ʿAwf ibn ʿĀmir in Banū ʿĀmir. It describes them as their soothsayers and leaders. Al-Jalālayn calls them *their devils, their leaders.* **What they said.** Muḥammad ibn Isḥāq reported that Ibn ʿAbbās said the verse means: *we are with you — verily we were but mocking*, that is, we only mock the believers and deceive them. Ad-Daḥḥāk said that Ibn ʿAbbās read it as *we, the hypocrites, were mocking the Companions of Muḥammad.* Ar-Rabīʿ ibn Anas and Qatādah said the same. Al-Jalālayn adds a note on the recitation that shows how closely the classical commentators read: *laqū* is actually *laquyū*, but the *ḍamma* has been omitted as too cumbersome for pronunciation, and the *yāʾ* is dropped because it is unvocalised and followed by a *wāw*. **The mockery is answered in the same word.** Ibn Kathīr makes the structural point that gives this verse its weight. Allah states that He will punish the hypocrites for their mockery *using the same terms to describe both the deed and its punishment, although the meaning is different.* As-Suddī reported that Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn Masʿūd and several other Companions said that *and He leaves them increasing* means He gives them respite. Mujāhid said: He causes their deviation to increase. And Ibn Jarīr commented that the correct meaning is *We give them increase, in the sense of giving them respite and leaving them in their deviation and rebellion.* So the hypocrites said *we were mocking*, and the reply uses the same verb of God — but where their mockery was a lie told to companions, His is the letting-alone of people who have already decided. That is the same pattern verse ten established with the disease. The punishment is not something added from outside. It is the condition allowed to run. **What the mockery actually was.**

*We were only mocking* is the most revealing phrase in the section, and it is worth sitting with.

Mockery is not disagreement. The open disbelievers of 2:6–7 rejected the message and were described as sealed. These people accepted it often enough to repeat it, and then treated the repetition as a joke performed for an audience.

Al-Mukhtaṣar gives the motive for both rooms in one line: they say *we believe what you believe* to the believers *because they think it will benefit them to act this way*, and to their leaders they say *we are really with you and follow you.* Neither statement is offered as a conviction. Both are instruments.

That is why the verse calls their associates *shayāṭīn*. The word is not primarily a moral slur. It marks the people whose approval they actually wanted — and the verse's structure says that the room where they were sincere was the room where they mocked.

**The verse that follows answers it in the same vocabulary.**

Ibn Kathīr's point about Allah describing both the deed and its punishment in the same terms is not a curiosity. It is the hinge into the next verse.

The hypocrites said *we were mocking*. The reply, in the verse that follows, uses the same verb of God. And the commentators are careful about what that verb means when it is God's: as-Suddī, from Ibn ʿAbbās and Ibn Masʿūd and several other Companions, explains that *and He leaves them increasing* means He gives them respite. Mujāhid says He causes their deviation to increase. Ibn Jarīr concludes that the correct meaning is *We give them increase, in the sense of giving them respite and leaving them in their deviation and rebellion.*

So the answer to mockery is not a counter-mockery. It is being left alone with what you chose.

That is precisely the mechanism verse ten described as disease increasing. The two verses are one argument in two movements: the condition, and then what it looks like when God stops interrupting it.

**Why the private room is quoted at all.**

Nothing in the verse is hidden from God, and the sūrah says so twice already — 2:9 that Allah knows what is secret and has told the believers what these people are like, 2:10 that the disease is in the heart where no one else can see it.

Quoting the private conversation therefore does something other than exposing a secret. It shows the reader the two statements together, in the hypocrites' own words, and lets the contradiction stand without comment. Verse eleven reported their public claim; verse twelve refused it in one line; verse thirteen reported their contempt for the believers; and now this verse supplies what they said when they thought it was safe.

The sūrah never needs to say *they were lying.* It only has to put both sentences on the page.

**Why thirteen verses for this group.** Maʿārif's structural note explains the proportion, and it is worth having before the section continues. Al-Baqarah opens by declaring the Qurʾān beyond all doubt. Its first twenty verses delineate those who believe in it and those who do not: the first five deal with the believers, under the title *al-muttaqūn*; the next two with the disbelievers who were open and violent in their hostility, *al-kāfirūn*; and the following thirteen with the crafty disbelievers who claimed to be Muslims but were not — who receive from the Qurʾān the name *al-munāfiqūn*. Two verses for open hostility, thirteen for concealed hostility. The sūrah is not mainly concerned with the enemy who attacks. It is concerned with the one who says *we believe* in one room and *we were only mocking* in another. **The verse in one line.** They have two audiences and two messages, and they think the second is safe because the first is believed. The verse exists because neither is hidden — and because, as verse ten said, the person who arranges his life this way cannot see what he has become.

15.text:
*Allah will throw their mockery back at them, leaving them to continue wandering blindly in their defiance.* The verse answers the question verse fourteen left open. They said *we were only mocking.* Now it says what happens to the mockery.

**The same verb, changed sides.**

The word used here is built on the same root as their own *nastahziʾ* in verse fourteen. They mocked; the verse says the mocking comes back.

Ibn Kathīr's point — which he sets up in the previous verse and completes here — is that the verse describes a punishment that matches the crime in its very form. Not a heavier version of it, but the same act, reversed.

Al-Jalālayn puts the mechanism plainly: *God Himself mocks them, requiting them for their mockery.* It is not a new offence. It is a payment.

**What that mockery is.**

Tanwīr al-Miqbās gives it a specific shape, and it is the only one of the six sources that does: *He will open a gate of Paradise for them and then shut it before their eyes, and so the believers will mock them.*

Read that carefully. The reversal is total. In verse fourteen the hypocrites had an audience — their own leaders, in their own room, performing a joke for people whose approval they wanted. Here the audience is still there, but it has changed sides. The people being laughed at are now the ones laughing.

Al-Mukhtaṣar supplies the two-timeframe version of the same thing: they are treated as believers in this world, but will be repaid for their lying and deception in the next life. Which is why the gate can be opened at all — it is opened because, outwardly, they qualified.

**The long rope.**

Maʿārif's reading is the one that explains why the delay happened. *Since the hypocrites saw no apparent signs of divine punishment descending on themselves, they were encouraged in their complacency and rebellion, so that the cup of their iniquity was full, and one day they were caught.*

Allah has, in His forbearance and mercy, given them a long rope — but the rope is a provision for their being thrown into ridicule.

That is the answer to the obvious objection, which is that the delay looks like success. It reads as evidence that they got away with it. Maʿārif's account says the opposite: the delay is part of the sentence, not an exemption from it. Every month of impunity added weight to what was accumulating.

**Wandering blindly.**

The final phrase, *yaghmahūn*, is what they are left doing. Al-Jalālayn glosses it as *bewildered, wavering in perplexity*, and notes a grammatical detail worth keeping: it is a circumstantial qualifier. The wandering is not something that happens to them afterwards. It is the state they are in *while* the respite runs.

Tanwīr al-Miqbās draws the same line but locates it in this world: *He will leave them in this world blind in their disbelief and error, unable to see either faith or guidance.*

So the mockery has two halves and two times. Here: a long rope, and confusion inside it. There: a gate, and a shut door.

Al-Mukhtaṣar compresses both into one clause — He allows them to become more and more lost and to do more and more wrong, so they remain confused and doubtful about the truth. Which is exactly the disease of 2:10 still increasing, now described from the outside.

16.text:
*They are the ones who trade guidance for misguidance. But this trade is profitless, and they are not rightly guided.*

**A purchase, not a mistake.**

The verse uses the vocabulary of commerce — *ishtara*, bought; *tijārah*, trade; *rabiḥat*, made a profit. That is a deliberate choice, and the commentators read it as one.

A mistake is something that happens to you. A purchase is something you do. Nobody buys by accident.

Maʿārif draws out the insult inside the metaphor: *In giving the name of "trade" or "commerce" to this action, the Holy Qurʾān suggests that these worldly-wise men had no understanding even of the art of trading.* They were the people of Madinah who could calculate. The verse says they could not calculate.

**What the early commentators said they bought.**

Ibn Kathīr collects three readings, and they are not competing explanations so much as three descriptions of one act:

- **As-Suddī**, reporting from **Ibn ʿAbbās** and **Ibn Masʿūd**: *They pursued misguidance and abandoned guidance.*
- **Mujāhid**: *They believed and then disbelieved.*
- **Qatādah**: *They preferred deviation to guidance.*

Ibn Kathīr then does something useful — he shows these are compatible. The verse *includes those who first believed, then later disbelieved*, and he cites 63:3 for them: *That is because they believed, and then disbelieved; therefore their hearts are sealed.* And it also includes those who simply preferred deviation over guidance.

*The hypocrites fall into several categories*, he says. That matters, because verse 17 and verse 19 will give two different parables, and Maʿārif will explain that the two parables describe two different kinds of person.

**Qatādah's comparison.**

Ibn Kathīr sets Qatādah's wording next to 41:17, about Thamūd: *And as for Thamūd, We granted them guidance, but they preferred blindness to guidance.*

The verb there — *istaḥabbū*, they loved, they preferred — is the same shape of choice. Guidance was offered and available. It was declined in favour of something worse, on purpose.

And **Ibn Jarīr** records Qatādah saying of this very verse: *By Allah! I have seen them leaving guidance for deviation, leaving the community of the believers for the sects.* Not a theory about seventh-century Madinah. A report from someone watching it happen.

**Why the trade fails.**

*This trade is profitless, and they are not rightly guided.* Two losses, and they are different losses.

Al-Jalālayn spells out the arithmetic: *they have gained nothing from it — indeed they have lost, because their destination is the Fire made everlasting for them; nor are they guided in what they did.*

A bad trade normally still leaves you holding something. You overpaid, but you have the goods. Here there are no goods. Tanwīr al-Miqbās: *they did not prosper in their bargain but on the contrary were not guided to overcome their error.*

Al-Mukhtaṣar names what was lost on each side: *they lost their faith in Allah and lost the way to the truth.* Both. Not one for the other.

Maʿārif adds the detail that makes it absurd rather than merely unfortunate: *they had grown up in a pagan society, and knew very well what the way of the infidels was. Now they had become familiar enough with Islam too, and could easily see the difference.* This was not a man choosing between two unfamiliar options. He had used both and knew which was which.

So the verse is not saying they were deceived. It is saying they shopped, compared, and picked wrong — and the last clause denies them even the consolation of having been lost along the way. *They are not rightly guided.* They knew the road.

17.text:
*Their example is that of someone who kindles a fire, but when it lights up all around them, Allah takes away their light, leaving them in complete darkness—unable to see.*

**Why the sūrah switches to pictures.**

For six verses — 2:8 to 2:13 — the sūrah described the hypocrites by what they said and did. From here it stops arguing and starts showing.

Al-Mukhtaṣar names the structure: *Allah shows us what the hypocrites are like with two examples: one related to fire, and the other to water.* Maʿārif explains why two: *The choice of two examples is meant to divide the hypocrites into two kinds of men.* That is the key to verses 17–20, and it is why the sūrah does not stop after one picture.

**The man and the fire.**

Tanwīr al-Miqbās gives the scene its motive, which the verse leaves implicit: the man *lights a fire in the darkness in order to provide safety for his family, his property and his person.*

That is worth pausing on. This is not a bonfire for warmth or a signal fire. It is a man protecting what he is responsible for, at night, in the open. The fire is a considered, sensible, competent act.

*And when it sheddeth its light around him* — Tanwīr continues — *he sees what is around him and feels secure.*

Al-Jalālayn adds the third benefit the fire brings: *so that he is able to see and to feel warm and secure from those he feared.*

Light. Warmth. Safety. The verse gives him all three, and gives them to him completely — *it lights up all around him*, not in one corner.

**Then it goes out.**

Ibn Kathīr describes the moment: *When the fire was lit, and illuminated the surrounding area, the person benefited from it and felt safe. Then the fire was suddenly extinguished. Therefore, total darkness covered this person, and he became unable to see anything or find his way out of it.*

*Suddenly* is doing real work there. There was no warning, no wind building, no slow fading. He was safe and then he was not.

And notice what the darkness is made worse by. Ibn Kathīr: *Allah removed what benefits them, and this is the light, and He left them with what harms them, that is, the darkness and the smoke.*

Smoke. A fire that is still there but no longer lighting anything. Al-Mukhtaṣar catches this too — *it goes out, smouldering and leaving him in the dark.* The thing that was supposed to help is now the thing making it worse, because he cannot see, and there is smoke, and he cannot even tell where the fire is.

**The pronoun that shifts.**

Al-Jalālayn flags a detail in the Arabic that most readers pass over. The verse says *the one who kindled* — singular — and then *Allah takes away **their** light*, plural. His note: *the plural pronoun in nūrihim takes into account the plural import of alladhī.*

The word for "the one who" is grammatically singular but carries a general sense — anyone who does this. The plural is what the verse is actually pointing at. The man is not a character in a story. He is a shape that many people fit.

**What each element means.**

Ibn Kathīr maps the parable directly:

- **The fire** is guidance — *this parable indicates that the hypocrites first believed, then disbelieved.*
- **The darkness** is *their doubts, disbelief and hypocrisy.*
- **Unable to see** means *they are unable to find the correct path or find its direction.*

Al-Jalālayn's mapping is sharper about the timing: *likewise are those who have found temporary security by professing faith but who will meet with terror and punishment upon death.*

That is the point of the suddenness. The fire did not go out while he was watching and able to relight it. It went out at the moment he most needed it and could no longer do anything about it.

**The hardest line in the parable.**

*Taraka-hum* — He left them. Ibn Kathīr takes it literally and does not soften it: Allah *left them with what harms them.*

This is the same verb the previous unit ended on. Verse 15 said Allah leaves them *wandering blindly in their defiance*; verse 14 said He leaves them *increasing in their mockery*. The word has now appeared three times in six verses, and each time it means the same thing: not punishment arriving, but help being withdrawn.

**Why the verse cannot end here.**

Al-Mukhtaṣar closes the picture: *Such people then remain in the dark, unable to see anything or find a way.*

That is a complete image, and the sūrah immediately adds to it. The next verse describes the man as deaf, dumb and blind — which is more than darkness explains. A man in the dark can still hear and call out. Verse 18 says this one cannot.

Ibn Kathīr links them himself, and in doing so quotes 22:46: *Verily, it is not the eyes that grow blind, but it is the hearts which are in the breasts that grow blind.* The parable is about sight, but the sūrah is not talking about eyes. It never was.

18.text:
*They are wilfully deaf, dumb, and blind, so they will never return to the Right Path.*

**Four words, and a disagreement about one of them.**

Three nouns, no verb. Arabic can do this — a sentence that simply states what something is. There is no "they became" or "they were made." Just: deaf, dumb, blind.

Tanwīr al-Miqbās reads all three as performance: *Deaf — pretending to be deaf. Dumb — pretending to be dumb. And blind — pretending to be blind.*

That is consistent with everything the unit has said about them. These are people whose entire position is a performance.

Al-Jalālayn and Al-Mukhtaṣar read them as description rather than pretence, and each attaches the deficit to a specific function. Al-Jalālayn: *deaf to the truth, so that they cannot hear it and accept it; dumb — mute as regards goodness, unable to speak of it; and blind to the path of guidance, so that they cannot perceive it.*

The three are not random disabilities. They are the three things a person needs in order to respond to a message: to take it in, to say something about it, and to find their way by it.

Tazkīrul al-Qurʾān makes exactly this connection, across its run covering 2:14–18: *They have eyes, but cannot see; they have ears, but cannot hear; they have tongues, but cannot speak. They can neither hear the call of truth, nor respond to it in any way, nor can they find their way by any sign from God.*

**Why the order matters.**

Ibn Kathīr keeps the sequence and explains it in the same order the verse gives it: *they are deaf, and thus cannot hear the guidance; dumb, and cannot utter the words that might benefit them; blind, in total darkness and deviation.*

Hearing comes first because it is the entry point. Nothing gets in. Speaking comes second because nothing comes out. Sight comes last because there is nowhere left to go.

And this follows verse 17's parable exactly. Ibn Kathīr says of the man whose fire went out that *this person could not hear or speak and became so blind that even if there were light, he would not be able to see.*

That last clause is the harshest thing said about them in the whole unit. Even with light. The problem is no longer the dark.

**They will never return.**

Al-Jalālayn: *they shall not return from error.* Tanwīr al-Miqbās: *so they return not from their disbelief and error.*

Ibn Kathīr explains why, and it is the verse's real subject: *this is why they cannot get back to the state that they were in before this happened to him.*

Before. The word assumes there was a before — which is Mujāhid's reading of verse 16, *they believed and then disbelieved*, and Ibn Kathīr's own note that the fire parable *indicates that the hypocrites first believed, then disbelieved.*

These people are not described as never having had anything. They had the fire. It lit up everything around them. And the verse says the loss is not recoverable, because the faculties that would have to recover it are the ones that are gone.

19.text:
*Or those caught in a rainstorm from the sky with darkness, thunder, and lightning. They press their fingers into their ears at the sound of every thunder-clap for fear of death. And Allah encompasses the disbelievers by His might.*

**The second picture, and why there are two.**

Maʿārif's explanation of the pair is the clearest thing written about these four verses, and it identifies two different groups:

*On the one hand were those in whom disbelief had taken deep roots, so that they had little inclination towards Islam, but pretended to be Muslims for worldly motives — the Holy Qurʾān compares them to the man who, having found light, again loses it, and is left in darkness.*

*On the other hand were those who did recognize the truth of Islam, and sometimes wished to be genuine Muslims, but worldly interests would not allow them to do so, and they remained in a perpetual state of hesitation and doubt — they have been likened to the men caught in a thunderstorm who move forward a step or two when there is a flash of lightning, but, when it is over, again get stuck.*

Ibn Kathīr opens with the same division: *This is another parable which Allah gave about the hypocrites who sometimes know the truth and doubt it at other times.*

So the fire was for those who had nothing left. The storm is for those who still flicker.

**What ṣayyib means — a real disagreement, recorded.**

Ibn Kathīr lists the authorities who say the word means **rain**: **Ibn Masʿūd**, **Ibn ʿAbbās** and several other Companions, then **Abū al-ʿĀliyah**, **Mujāhid**, **Saʿīd ibn Jubayr**, **ʿAṭāʾ**, **al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī**, **Qatādah**, **ʿAṭiyyah al-ʿAwfī**, **ʿAṭāʾ al-Khurāsānī**, **As-Suddī** and **Ar-Rabīʿ ibn Anas**.

Against them: **Ad-Daḥḥāk** said *it is the clouds.*

Ibn Kathīr's verdict: *the most accepted opinion is that it means the rain.*

Al-Jalālayn gives the linguistics behind the word, which settles why "rain" reads better than "cloud": *ka-ṣayyib — the term is originally ṣayyūb, from the verb ṣāba yaṣūbu, meaning "it came down."* The word is built from falling, not from gathering.

**A storm at night.**

Tanwīr al-Miqbās sets the scene with two details the verse does not state: *the likeness of the hypocrites and the Jews with respect to the Qurʾān is like rain that has poured down from heaven at night onto the wilderness.*

At night. In open country. Rain in daylight is an inconvenience. Rain at night in the open, with no shelter, is something else — and the verse has already stacked darkness on top of it.

**What each part of the storm is.**

Ibn Kathīr: **darkness** is *the doubts, disbelief and hypocrisy*. **Thunder** is *what shocks the hearts with fear*. **Lightning** is *the light of faith that is sometimes felt in the hearts of the hypocrites.*

On thunder he brings in two other verses to show this is a settled description of them, not an inference. 63:4 — *They think that every cry is against them.* And 9:56–57 — *They swear by Allah that they are truly of you while they are not of you, but they are a people who are afraid. Should they find refuge, or caves, or a place of concealment, they would turn straightway thereto in a swift rush.*

Tanwīr al-Miqbās maps the same three onto the Qurʾān itself: it *contains darkness as embodied in the exposition of seditions, thunderings of rebuke whereby fear is instilled, lightning of exposition, instruction and promise.*

Al-Jalālayn does the mapping in one movement: *similar is the case with these, when the Qurʾān is revealed in which there is mention of the unbelief — that is like darkness — the threat of punishment, that is like the sound of thunder, and the clear arguments, that are like the clear lightning. They shut their ears in order not to hear it, and thereby incline towards true faith and abandon their religion, which for them would be death.*

That last clause is the hinge of the whole verse, and it inverts everything.

**They fear the wrong death.**

*They press their fingers into their ears at the sound of every thunder-clap for fear of death.*

Al-Jalālayn has just said that what they actually fear — hearing the Qurʾān and being drawn to faith — is what they call *death*. And what they are protecting themselves from, by blocking their ears, is life.

Tanwīr al-Miqbās says the same of the historical scene: *the Jews and hypocrites used to put their fingers in their ears when they heard the Qurʾān recited, delivering promises and threats like thunder-claps, and this they did for fear of death, i.e. for fear of being drawn to it.*

Tazkīrul Qurʾān generalises it, and this is the verse's application to anyone reading it: *God's word as revealed to His prophets affects them similarly. On the one hand, it holds out to man the promise of great success, but on the other hand, its acceptance places man temporarily at risk: there is the fear of losing one's worldly position; of clashing with the conventional set-up. Fear of these things sometimes makes one halt, and sometimes makes one move hesitantly on. But such caution cannot help one.*

Rain is a blessing. So is revelation. The storm is not the punishment — the punishment is being unable to stand in the rain.

**The verse's closing line.**

*And Allah encompasses the disbelievers by His might.*

Al-Jalālayn: *God encompasses the disbelievers in both knowledge and power, so they cannot escape Him.* Tanwīr al-Miqbās: *He knows them and will gather them in Hell.* Al-Mukhtaṣar: *Allah surrounds the disbelievers, and has absolute power over them, so they cannot escape Him.*

After a verse about people covering their ears to avoid something, this is the answer. You can block the sound. You cannot leave the enclosure.

20.text:
*It is as if the lightning were about to snatch away their sight. Whenever lightning strikes, they walk in its light, but when darkness covers them, they stand still. Had Allah willed, He could have taken away their hearing and sight. Surely Allah is Most Capable of everything.*

**The middle of the verse is the whole hypocrite.**

*Whenever lightning strikes, they walk in its light, but when darkness covers them, they stand still.*

Maʿārif's description of this second group — the ones the storm pictures — is precise: they *move forward a step or two when there is a flash of lightning, but, when it is over, again get stuck.*

That is not a description of an unbeliever. An unbeliever does not move when the lightning flashes. This is somebody who genuinely responds, and then stops, and then responds again.

Al-Jalālayn reads the movement as interior rather than physical: *a simile of the perturbation that the Qurʾānic arguments cause in their hearts, and of their acknowledging the truths of what they love to hear and recoiling from what they detest.*

They walk when the argument suits them. They stop when it does not.

**Why the lightning is unbearable.**

*It is as if the lightning were about to snatch away their sight.*

The verb — *yakhaṭifu*, to snatch, to grab and run — is the same one used in 24:43 of lightning snatching sight. It is violent and fast.

Al-Jalālayn: *the lightning almost snatches away their sight, that is, takes it away swiftly.*

Ibn Kathīr has already identified the lightning as *the light of faith that is sometimes felt in the hearts of the hypocrites*. So the thing that lets them see is also the thing that hurts them. That is not a flaw in the parable. It is the point.

**Tanwīr's reading of the ending — and it is the bleakest in the six.**

*Likewise, when the hypocrites declared themselves to be believers, they went along with that which the believers went along with, because their outward faith was accepted. But when they died, they remained in the darkness of the grave.*

Tanwīr al-Miqbās takes *when darkness covers them, they stand still* as a description of death. The walking was the lifetime. The standing still is what came after, and there is no further lightning scheduled.

**The two faculties, and what has already happened to them.**

*Had Allah willed, He could have taken away their hearing and sight.*

Al-Jalālayn's gloss is the sharpest sentence in the whole unit: *had God willed, He would have taken away their hearing and their sight — that is, the exterior faculty — in the same way that He took away their inner one.*

The inner one is already gone. Verse 18 said deaf, dumb, blind. This verse says only that the outer version has not yet followed.

Al-Mukhtaṣar makes the condition explicit: *If God willed, He could take away their hearing and their sight, in His absolute power over all things, and not return it to them, because they turn away from the truth.*

Tanwīr al-Miqbās attaches each faculty to its cause in the storm: *if Allah willed, He could take away the hearing of the hypocrites and the Jews through the rebukes and threats contained in the Qurʾān, and He could also take away their sight through the exposition contained therein.*

**Why the verse closes on power.**

*Surely Allah is Most Capable of everything.* Al-Jalālayn: *Truly God has power over all things that He wills, as for example His taking away of the above-mentioned.*
