Similarly, in the Islamic Sharīʿah too, certain major sins necessarily entail capital punishment even when the sinner has offered this tawbah — for example, life in return for a life in the case of intentional homicide, or death by stoning in the case of adultery established through proper evidence.*

Repentance does not cancel every consequence. That is the point he is making, and it is the same point the verse makes.

**Forgiven on both sides.**

The last clause of Ibn ʿAbbās's report is the one that settles the difficulty: *So Allah forgave both the killer and the killed.*

The men who carried out the command were not exempt from the sin — they had worshipped the calf too, or they would not have been in the camp. And the men who died under it were not merely executed. Both groups are named as forgiven.

That is why the verse can list this among the favours. It was not a purge. It was a repentance that happened to cost lives, and everyone in it came out the other side pardoned.

**Then He accepted your repentance.**

*Fa-tāba ʿalaykum.* Tanwīr al-Miqbās: *He will relent towards you — He will forgive you. Lo! He is the Relenting towards the penitent, the Merciful towards any that die repentant.*

Al-Jalālayn notes the order, and it is the same one he noted at 2:37: *and He will turn to you, relenting, before your turning in repentance.*

Allah's turning comes first. That is what makes the repentance possible.

Al-Mukhtaṣar: *So, you did this with Allah's approval, and He forgave you, for He is Forgiving and Merciful with His servants.*

**Why the verse is a favour.**

Maʿārif closes the loop: *Then the Israelites acted upon these divine commandments, they became worthy of receiving the mercy and favour of Allah in the other world.*

The verse sits in a list of blessings — after the rescue from Pharaoh, the sea, the forty nights, the Torah. A command to kill your own people is listed among the favours.

The reason is in the last clause. *Surely He is the Accepter of Repentance, Most Merciful.* A way back was opened. That is the favour. The cost was severe, and it was still mercy.

55.text:
*And remember when you said, "O Moses! We will never believe you until we see Allah with our own eyes," so a thunderbolt struck you while you were looking on.*

**Maʿārif's account of how they got there.**

This is the fullest narrative in the six sources, and it explains a demand that otherwise looks absurd:

*Then Sayyidunā Mūsā brought the Torah from Mount Ṭūr (Sinai) and presented it to the Israelites as the book of Allah. Some of them were insolent enough to say that they could not believe it until and unless Allah Himself told them in so many words. With the permission of Allah, Sayyidunā Mūsā replied that even this condition would be fulfilled, if they went with him to Mount Ṭūr. The Israelites chose seventy men for this purpose. Arriving there, they heard the words of Allah with their own ears.*

*Now, in their perversity, they invented a new ruse. It was not enough, they said, to hear the speech, for they could not be sure whether it was Allah Himself who had spoken to them or someone else. But they promised that they would be finally convinced if they could see Allah with their own eyes. Since it is beyond the power of a living being to be able to see Allah in the physical world, they had to pay for their impertinence, and were killed by a thunderbolt.*

They heard Allah speak. And then asked for identification.

Al-Jalālayn sets the same scene: *having gone out with Mūsā to apologise before God for your worship of the calf, and having heard what he had said to you.*

So these seventy were the delegation sent to repent for verse 54 — and they used the occasion to make a new demand.

**See Allah plainly.**

*Ḥattā nara allāha jahratan.* Ibn ʿAbbās defined the word: *means "publicly", "so that we gaze at Allah."*

Al-Jalālayn: *we will not believe you till we see God openly, with our own eyes.*

Tanwīr al-Miqbās gives the comparison they were making: *until we see Allah plainly, until we see Him plainly as you did.*

*As you did.* That is the actual objection. They were not asking for a miracle. They were asking for parity with Mūsā.

**"We will never believe you."**

*Lan nuʾmina laka.* Not "we doubt." A flat refusal with a condition attached that they knew — or should have known — could not be met.

Al-Mukhtaṣar describes the tone: *when you shamelessly addressed Mūsā, saying that you would not believe him until you saw Allah with your own eyes, in the open before you.*

**The thunderbolt.**

*Aṣ-ṣāʿiqah.* As-Suddī described what happened next, and Ibn Kathīr records it with Mūsā's prayer:

*"They died, and Mūsā stood up crying and supplicating to Allah, 'O Lord! What should I say to the Children of Israel when I go back to them after You destroyed the best of them? If it had been Your will, You could have destroyed them and me before; would You destroy us for the deeds of the foolish ones among us?' (7:150)"*

*The best of them.* These were the seventy chosen men.

Then the detail that reframes it: *Allah revealed to Mūsā that these seventy men were among those who worshipped the calf.*

**While you were looking on.**

*Wa antum tanẓurūn.* There are two readings, and they differ sharply.

**ʿUrwah ibn Ruwaym** said: *"Some of them were struck with lightning while others were watching." Allah resurrected those, and struck the others with lightning.*

Al-Jalālayn: *and the thunderbolt — the shout — took you, and you died, while you were beholding what was happening to you.*

Tanwīr al-Miqbās: *and even while you gazed, the lightning seized you — the Fire burnt you while you were looking at it.*

On one reading they watched each other die. On the other they watched themselves being struck.

Ibn Kathīr states the theological limit that the demand ran into: *Remember My favor on you for resurrecting you after you were seized with lightning when you asked to see Me directly, which neither you nor anyone else can bear or attain. This was said by Ibn Jurayj.*

**What the verse is doing in a list of favours.**

It is the second verse in a row about a punishment — verse 54's execution, and now this. And both are framed as blessings.

The reason is the same in both cases. A line was crossed, a consequence followed, and then verse 56 says *We brought you back to life*. The favour is not the thunderbolt. It is what came after it.

Al-Mukhtaṣar's summary: *and the lightning struck you and killed you, whilst some of you looked at the others.*

56.text:
*Then We brought you back to life after your death, so that perhaps you would be grateful.*

**The shortest verse in the sequence, and the one that makes the previous two favours.**

Verse 54 ended on forgiveness. Verse 55 ended on death. This verse reverses the death in eleven words.

Al-Jalālayn: *Then We raised you up, brought you back to life, after you were dead, so that you might be thankful for this favour of Ours.*

Tanwīr al-Miqbās: *Then We revived you — We brought you back to life — after your death, after burning you, that ye might give thanks — that you might give thanks that I brought you back to life.*

**Why they were brought back.**

Maʿārif gives the reason, and it is not the reason people expect:

*This verse refers to death, which suggests that the thunderbolt had killed them. Since the Israelites had always been mistrusting Sayyidunā Mūsā, he feared that they would suspect him of having taken the men to a solitary place and got them slaughtered. So, he prayed to Allah to save him from such a vile accusation. Allah granted his prayer, and gave those a new life.*

The resurrection protected Mūsā's reputation. Seventy men went up a mountain with him and came back — or the whole community would have concluded he had killed them.

That connects directly to verse 55's prayer, which Ibn Kathīr recorded through As-Suddī: *O Lord! What should I say to the Children of Israel when I go back to them after You destroyed the best of them?*

**How it happened.**

As-Suddī's account, again via Ibn Kathīr: *Afterwards, Allah brought them back to life one man at a time, while the rest of them were watching how Allah was bringing them back to life.*

One at a time, with the others watching. That is what *while you were looking on* in verse 55 turns out to mean on this reading — they watched the resurrection, not only the death.

**Ar-Rabīʿ ibn Anas on what the death was for.**

Ibn Kathīr records his position: *Death was their punishment, and they were resurrected after they died so they could finish out [their lives].*

Not a demonstration. A sentence, served, and then commuted.

**So that perhaps you would be grateful.**

*Laʿallakum tashkurūn.* The same particle as verse 52, and Maʿārif's explanation from there applies here too — it expresses what onlookers expect of a man who has been pardoned, not any uncertainty in Allah.

Grateful for what, specifically? Tanwīr al-Miqbās: *that you might give thanks that I brought you back to life.*

**The pattern the sūrah is establishing.**

Verses 54 to 56 run: command, execution, forgiveness. Demand, thunderbolt, resurrection.

Each failure is followed immediately by restoration, and each restoration is listed among the favours. That is the structure of the whole address to the Children of Israel, and verse 57 continues it into the wilderness.

Al-Mukhtaṣar: *Then He brought you back to life after death, so that you might be thankful to Him for the blessings He granted you in this way.*

And the verse does one more thing quietly. It is the second resurrection this sūrah has described — 2:28 said *He will cause you to die and again bring you to life*. That was general and future. This one happened, to seventy named men, in front of witnesses.

57.text:
*And remember when We shaded you with clouds and sent down to you manna and quails, saying, "Eat from the good things We have provided for you." The evildoers certainly did not wrong Us, but wronged themselves.*

**Where this happened — and it is not where people assume.**

Maʿārif sets the geography, and it reframes the whole verse:

*These two incidents took place in the wilderness of Tīh. The Israelites belonged to Syria, but had gone to Egypt in the time of Sayyidunā Yūsuf, and settled there, while Syria itself had come under the domination of a people called the ʿAmāliqah (Amalekites). When the Pharaoh had been drowned and the Israelites could live in peace, Allah commanded them to go to war against the ʿAmāliqah, and to free their homeland. The Israelites started on the expedition, but, on approaching Syria, when they came to learn about the military strength of the foe, their courage failed them, and they refused to engage themselves in the jihād. Allah punished them for their disobedience, so that for full forty years they kept wandering about in a wilderness, and could not even go back to Egypt.*

*The wilderness was not very vast, but only a stretch of some ten miles, lying between Egypt and Syria. They would make a day-long march in the direction of Egypt, and stop somewhere for the night. But, on getting up the next morning, they would always find themselves just where they had started.*

Ten miles. Forty years. The cloud and the manna were not travel provisions. They were the supply line for a sentence.

**The cloud.**

*Al-ghamām.* Ibn Kathīr describes it: *This verse mentions the white clouds that provided shade for the Children of Israel, protecting them from the sun's heat during their years of wandering.*

Then the witnesses: *In the ḥadīth about the trials, an-Nasāʾī recorded Ibn ʿAbbās saying, "Allah shaded the Children of Israel with clouds during the years of wandering." Ibn Abī Ḥātim said, "Narrations similar to that of Ibn ʿAbbās were reported from Ibn ʿUmar, ar-Rabīʿ ibn Anas, Abū Mijlaz, ad-Daḥḥāk, and As-Suddī."*

Al-Ḥasan and Qatādah said: *This happened when they were in the desert, and the clouds shielded them from the sun.*

And Ibn Jarīr's note on what kind of cloud it was: *several scholars said that the type of cloud the verse mentioned "was cooler and better than the type we know."*

**The manna.**

ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥah reported that **Ibn ʿAbbās** said: *The manna used to descend to them to the trees, and they used to eat whatever they wished of it.*

Then Qatādah's description, which is the most detailed in the six sources:

*The manna, which was whiter than milk and sweeter than honey, used to rain down on the Children of Israel, just as the snow falls, from dawn until sunrise. One of them would collect enough for that particular day, for if it remained more than that, it would spoil. On the sixth day, Friday, one would collect enough for the sixth and the seventh day, which was the Sabbath, during which one would not leave home to seek his livelihood, or for anything else.*

A daily ration that spoiled if kept — except on Friday, when a double portion was allowed for the Sabbath.

Al-Jalālayn identifies it botanically: *manna and quails — which are respectively a type of citrus known as turanjubīn and the quail.* Al-Mukhtaṣar: *a sweet drink similar to honey.*

**Eat from the good things.**

*Kulū min ṭayyibāti mā razaqnākum.* Tanwīr al-Miqbās adds the condition attached to it: *Eat of the good things, of the lawful things, wherewith We have provided you — that We have given you — and do not keep any provision for future days.*

Al-Jalālayn records what they did with that instruction:

*And We said, "Eat of the good things We have provided for you," and do not store any of it away — but they were not grateful for this favour, and stored the food, and so they were deprived of it.*

They hoarded. And the hoarding ended the supply.

**They did not wrong Us.**

*Wa mā ẓalamūnā wa lākin kānū anfusahum yaẓlimūn.*

Al-Jalālayn: *And they did not wrong Us in this, but themselves they wronged, since the evil consequences of this befell them.*

Tanwīr al-Miqbās ties it to the specific act: *Yet they did save food for future days — "They wronged us not" by saving food, "but they did wrong themselves" — they harmed themselves.*

Al-Mukhtaṣar states the mechanism: *Their ingratitude and disbelief for these blessings did not affect Allah in any way, but they wronged themselves, losing their share from the good they had done and exposing themselves to suffering.*

**Why the verse ends there.**

It is the fourth time the sūrah has said this. 2:9 — *only they deceive themselves, but they fail to perceive*. 2:35 — *or else you will be wrongdoers*. 2:54 — *you have wronged yourselves*. And here.

Each time the point is identical: the damage lands on the one who does it. Allah loses nothing by being disobeyed.

Which is the whole argument of this address in one clause. They were given shade, food that fell from the sky, and a double portion on Friday. They stored it. And the loss was entirely theirs.

Tazkīrul Qurʾān's summary of the section states what they had instead:

*True piety is to worship God alone, to believe in Him though one has not seen Him, to live in fear of Judgement Day, to subsist on the pure things of the earth, to prevent whomsoever one can from falling into sin.*

*To believe in Him though one has not seen Him.* That is the direct answer to verse 55's demand. And *to subsist on the pure things of the earth* is the direct answer to this one.

58.text:
*And remember when We said, "Enter this city and eat freely from wherever you please; enter the gate with humility, saying, 'Absolve us.' We will forgive your sins and multiply the reward for the good-doers."*

**Which city.**

There is a real disagreement, and Ibn Kathīr sets out both sides.

*The correct opinion about the meaning of "the holy land" mentioned here is that it was Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem), as As-Suddī, ar-Rabīʿ ibn Anas, Qatādah and Abū Muslim al-Aṣfahānī, as well as others, have stated.*

Then the other view: *However, some scholars said that the holy land is Jericho (Arīḥāʾ), and this opinion was mentioned from Ibn ʿAbbās and ʿAbd ar-Raḥmān ibn Zayd.*

Al-Jalālayn holds both open in a single clause: *Enter this city — either the Holy House of Jerusalem, Bayt al-Maqdis, or Jericho, Arīḥā.*

Tanwīr al-Miqbās takes the second without qualification: *Go into this township — the village of Jericho (Arīḥā).*

**When it happened — and Maʿārif's warning about the question.**

Maʿārif sets out the two chronologies and then says something important about how to read the Qurʾān:

*There are two views as to when this incident took place. According to Shāh ʿAbd al-Qādir, when the Israelites grew weary of eating the same Mann and Salwā every day and prayed for being granted the kind of food they were used to (2:61), they were commanded to go to a certain city where they could get what they wished for. So, the commandment in the present verse pertains to the mode of entering this city, and lays down the spiritual etiquette for action and speech on this occasion.*

*On the other hand is the view that the commandment pertains to the city against which the Israelites had been ordered to engage themselves in a jihād. They obeyed it only after their long wanderings in the wilderness, and conquered the city. The commandment reported in verse 58 was sent to them through Sayyidunā Yūshaʿ (Joshua), who was the prophet among them at the time.*

On the first reading this verse comes after 2:61. On the second, decades later. And Maʿārif's conclusion:

*The discrepancy between the two views, which raises a question about the chronological sequence of the events, should not confuse us as to the nature of the stories narrated in the Holy Qurʾān. The Holy Qurʾān does not tell the stories for the sake of [chronology].*

**Ibn Kathīr's account of the conquest.**

*After the years of wandering ended forty years later, in the company of Yūshaʿ (Joshua) ibn Nūn, Allah allowed the Children of Israel to conquer the holy land on the eve of a Friday. On that day, the sun was kept from setting for a little more time, until victory was achieved.*

The sun held. That is the detail the verse leaves out and the tafsīr supplies.

**Eat freely from wherever you please.**

*Kulū minhā ḥaythu shiʾtum raghadā.* Al-Jalālayn: *and eat freely therein, wherever you will, plentifully and without any restrictions.*

Al-Mukhtaṣar: *abundantly consume, with ease, from the good things in it from any place you wanted.*

Tanwīr al-Miqbās: *and eat freely of that which is therein, whenever you will.*

The permission is total, and it is the same formula as 2:35 in Paradise — *eat as freely as you please*. A city, after a wilderness, described in the language of the Garden.

**Enter the gate with humility.**

*Udkhulū al-bāba sujjadan.* Al-Jalālayn: *and enter it at the gate, its gate, prostrating — bowing.*

Ibn Kathīr explains the posture's purpose: *they were commanded to enter its gate while prostrating, in appreciation [of the favour].*

Al-Mukhtaṣar: *He told you to prostrate in humility to Him when you entered, asking Him to remove your sins.*

Not a victory march. A prostration at the threshold.

Tazkīrul Qurʾān states what they did instead, and it is the verse's whole point: *They were given possession of a great city and told to enter it — not in a vainglorious manner — but in humility and repentance; but instead they started rejoicing in their victory.*

**Saying "Absolve us."**

*Ḥiṭṭah.* Maʿārif explains the word: *Allah had commanded the Israelites to keep, while entering the city, repeating the word ḥiṭṭah, which indicates repentance for one's sin and the request for pardon.*

Al-Jalālayn renders it: *and say, "our request is for an exoneration" — that is, "That we be exonerated from our transgressions."*

Tanwīr al-Miqbās gives two readings: *say: "Repentance" — i.e. say: "forgive our sins"; as it is also said that this means: say: "there is no god save Allah."*

One word. And verse 59 will be about what they did to it.

**We will forgive your sins and multiply the reward.**

Al-Jalālayn notes a variant in the first verb: *and We shall forgive — naghfir; a variant reading has one of the two passive forms, yughfar or tughfar, "they will be forgiven" — you your transgressions.*

Then the second half: *and We shall give more to those who are virtuous — through obedience — in terms of reward.*

Tanwīr al-Miqbās: *We will forgive your sins and increase for the right-doers — increase their good deeds.*

Two promises, and the second is the one people skip. Not only forgiveness. Increase.

**Why this verse is in the list of favours.**

It is a command, not a gift. But it sits among the blessings because of what it offers: a city after a wilderness, food without restriction, and a single word that would have covered every sin they had committed to that point.

The cost was one word and one posture. Verse 59 says what they paid instead.

59.text:
*But the wrongdoers changed the words they were commanded to say. So We sent down a punishment from the heavens upon them for their rebelliousness.*

**What they changed it to.**

Three sources record the replacement phrase, and they differ slightly — which is itself worth noting, since the whole verse is about altering words.

Al-Jalālayn: *Then the evildoers among them substituted a saying other than that which had been said to them, and said instead "A grain inside a hair," and entered the town dragging themselves on their rears.*

Al-Mukhtaṣar: *entered dragging themselves on their rears, saying, "A grain in a hair," mocking Allah's sacred law.*

Maʿārif gives both variants: *they replaced this word with another phrase by way of mockery, and started saying, ḥabbatun fī shaʿīrah — "grain in the midst of barley" — or ḥinṭatun, "wheat."*

Tanwīr al-Miqbās: *they disobeyed the command and said "Wheat!"*

Ḥiṭṭah became ḥinṭah. One letter. *Absolve us* became *wheat*.

**And how they entered.**

The posture was changed with the word. They were told to enter prostrating. Al-Jalālayn and Al-Mukhtaṣar both record that they *entered the town dragging themselves on their rears.*

They performed the prostration — inverted, as a joke. The command was obeyed in form and inverted in intent, which is precisely the failure verse 44 named in the scholars who preached righteousness and did not practise it.

**Why the verse says "the wrongdoers" instead of "you".**

Al-Jalālayn flags the shift and explains it:

*So We sent down upon the evildoers — the replacement of the second person of the previous verse with the overt identification in the third person, alladhīna ẓalamū, "the evildoers," is intended to emphasise the depravity of their action.*

Verse 58 addressed them directly. Verse 59 stops doing that. The switch to third person is the verse stepping back from them.

**The punishment.**

*Rijzan min as-samāʾ.* Al-Jalālayn: *wrath — a punishment of plague — from the heaven, for their wickedness, for deviating from obedience. And within a very short period of time, just under seventy thousand of them were dead.*

Tanwīr al-Miqbās: *and We sent down upon the evil-doers, who changed the word they were ordered to say, wrath — the plague — from Heaven, for their evildoing, for changing the commands they were ordered to fulfil.*

Maʿārif confirms the number and its source: *The punishment which descended on them was plague, that wiped out seventy thousand men (Qurṭubī).*

Then he adds a ḥadīth that reframes it: *In passing, we may recall a ḥadīth which says that plague is a punishment for the disobedient, and a blessing for the obedient.*

The same event, two meanings, depending on who it lands on.

Al-Mukhtaṣar states the charge: *because they trespassed over the limits of the law and disobeyed His command.*

**Maʿārif's ruling drawn from the verse.**

He takes it into jurisprudence, and it is the most consequential comment in the six sources:

*The Israelites were punished for having changed a word ordained by Allah, and substituted a phrase of their own invention, thus distorting the meaning itself. According to the consensus of the fuqahāʾ (Muslim jurists), a change in the words of the Holy Qurʾān, or of a ḥadīth, or of a divine commandment, which invents or distorts the actual meaning, is impermissible.*

The verse is read as establishing a rule about transmission, not merely recording a punishment. Changing the words *and* the meaning with them is what was punished.

**Why changing a word was punished at all.**

It is worth sitting with the scale of this. Seventy thousand people died over a word.

Not over a sin of appetite, not over violence, not over refusal to enter the city. Over substituting *wheat* for *absolve us*.

Al-Jalālayn's note about the pronoun shift answers part of it. The verse steps back from addressing them — *the evildoers* instead of *you* — because what they did was not a lapse in the middle of obedience. It was obedience performed as mockery. They did enter. They did prostrate. They did say a word. Every element was there and inverted.

Ma'arif's ruling draws the line precisely: what was punished was *a change in the words... which invents or distorts the actual meaning*. Not every alteration of wording. The kind that carries a different meaning with it.

**Why this verse follows verse 58 so closely.**

Verse 58 gave four things: a city, food, a posture, a word. Verse 59 says two of the four were altered — the word and the posture — and that the alteration cost seventy thousand lives.

Not the city. Not the food. The word and the posture. The two things that cost nothing to do correctly.

**Plague as the specific punishment.**

Why plague, and why from the sky?

Tanwīr al-Miqbās and al-Jalālayn both identify *rijz* here as plague specifically, not punishment in general. And plague arrives from above, without an army, without a siege, without anything for them to fight. Verse 58 had just given them a conquered city. Verse 59 takes seventy thousand of them out of it by something no wall stops.

The forty years of wandering had ended. They had the land. And the deaths came after the victory, not before it.

And the sūrah has now made its pattern unmistakable. Every favour is followed by what they did with it.

Al-Jalālayn's closing phrase gives the timescale: *within a very short period of time.*

60.text:
*And remember when Moses prayed for water for his people, We said, "Strike the rock with your staff." Then twelve springs gushed out, and each tribe knew its drinking place. We then said, "Eat and drink of Allah's provisions, and do not go about spreading corruption in the land."*

**The prayer.**

The verse opens with Mūsā asking, not with Allah giving. Ibn Kathīr keeps that order: *Remember My favor on you when I answered the supplication of your Prophet, Mūsā, when he asked Me to provide you with water.*

Al-Mukhtaṣar sets the scene: *when you were in the wilderness, and you suffered great thirst, so Mūsā prayed to his Lord and asked that He give you water.*

Maʿārif places it in the same wanderings as the last two verses: *This incident too belongs to the story of the wanderings of the Israelites in the wilderness. Parched with thirst, they requested Sayyidunā Mūsā to pray to Allah for water.*

**Which rock.**

Al-Jalālayn's description is the most specific in the six sources, and it is strange:

*Strike with your staff the rock — the one that ran off with his robe. A light, cube-like rock, about the size of a man's head, made of marble.*

Tanwīr al-Miqbās: *smite with your staff the rock — that you have with you. This was a rock given to him by Allah. It had twelve nipples that resemble the nipples of women, and upon striking each one of these a spring gushed therefrom.*

Ibn ʿAbbās's version, recorded by Ibn Kathīr, gives the geometry: *The Children of Israel had a square stone that Mūsā was commanded to strike with his staff, and, as a result, twelve springs burst out of that stone, three on each side. Each tribe was, therefore, designated a certain spring, and they used to drink from their springs. They never had to travel from their area; they would find the same bounty in the same manner they had in the first area.*

Three springs on each of four sides. Twelve. And the same arrangement wherever the camp moved.

**Why twelve.**

Maʿārif explains the number from the family:

*Twelve streams gushed forth out of the rock, one for each of the twelve tribes. Sayyidunā Yaʿqūb (Jacob) had twelve sons, and each had a large family of his own. So, the families were considered as tribes, each with its own administrative organisation and its own head. Hence, the number twelve.*

Al-Mukhtaṣar gives the practical reason for the division: *Allah made clear to each tribe which was their spring to drink from, so that there would be no conflict between you.*

*So that there would be no conflict.* Twelve springs for a camp of maybe two million people is not an engineering necessity. One spring would have flowed. The division was to stop them fighting over water.

Al-Jalālayn: *twelve fountains, equal to the number of tribes. Each people — each tribe among them — came to know their drinking-place, which they did not share with any of the others.*

**Eat and drink.**

Ibn Kathīr ties the food and the water together, and names what they came from: *You eat from the manna and the quails, and drink from the water that I provided for you, without any effort or hardship for you. So worship the One Who did this for you.*

Maʿārif agrees: *What they have been asked to eat is the Mann and the Salwā (manna and quails), and the water is, of course, the one which had come out of the rock.*

Al-Mukhtaṣar states the condition: *He told you to eat and drink from what He provided for you, without any effort or work from you.*

Tazkīrul Qurʾān draws out what the provision was *for*, and it is the sharpest observation on the verse:

*Divine provision was given to them in the form of manna and quails so that, free from the struggle for a livelihood, they would be able to devote themselves entirely to carrying out God's commandments; but they took to demanding spicy, cooked foods instead.*

The food was not a luxury. It was time. Verse 61 is them spending it.

**Do not spread corruption in the land.**

*Lā taʿthaw fī al-arḍ mufsidīn.* Ibn Kathīr's gloss is the best available: *"Do not return the favour by committing acts of disobedience that cause favours to disappear."*

Maʿārif defines the word in context: *The Israelites have, in this verse, been asked not to spread disorder, which in this context signifies disobedience to Allah and transgression of His Commandments.*

Al-Jalālayn gives the grammar: *mufsidīn is a circumstantial qualifier emphasising its operator; the subject of the verb lā taʿthaw, "do not be degenerate," is derived from ʿathiya, meaning afsada, "to corrupt."*

Tanwīr al-Miqbās: *And do not act corruptly, making mischief in the earth — and do not cause mischief on the earth, or act contrary to what Mūsā commanded.*

This is the fifth time the sūrah has used the phrase — 2:11, 2:27, and now here. Each time it means the same thing: undoing what Allah has set in order.

**Al-Bayḍāwī on the miracle.**

Maʿārif records a comment from the great commentator al-Qāḍī al-Bayḍāwī, and it is the same argument he made at verse 50:

*Al-Qāḍī al-Bayḍāwī points out that it is a great error to deny miracles. When Allah has given a certain stone the unusual property of drawing iron to itself, it cannot be, logically and rationally speaking, impossible that He should [make water flow from it].*

A magnet is a stone that does something stones do not do. If that is granted, twelve springs are not a larger problem.

**The verse's place.**

Verses 58 and 59 were a city and a plague. This verse goes back to the wilderness and gives water. The sūrah is not running in strict order — Maʿārif said so at verse 58 — but it is running in one direction: favour, failure, favour, failure.

And the favour here is the largest yet. Not rescue from an enemy, not a word of pardon. Water, for twelve tribes, for forty years, from a stone the size of a man's head.

61.text:
*And remember when you said, "O Moses! We cannot endure the same meal every day. So just call upon your Lord on our behalf, He will bring forth for us some of what the earth produces of herbs, cucumbers, garlic, lentils, and onions." Moses scolded them, "Do you exchange what is better for what is worse? You can go down to any village and you will find what you have asked for." They were stricken with disgrace and misery, and they invited the displeasure of Allah for rejecting Allah's signs and unjustly killing the prophets. This is a fair reward for their disobedience and violations.*

**The longest verse so far, and the turning point of the address.**

Verses 49 to 60 have been a list of favours with failures attached. This one ends the list and states the verdict.

**What they asked for.**

Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī explained the complaint, and Ibn Kathīr records it: *"They were bored and impatient with the type of food they were provided. They also remembered the life they used to live, when their diet consisted of lentils, onions, garlic and herbs."*

Ibn Kathīr continues: *"One kind of food" — meaning the manna and quails, because they ate the same food day after day.*

Al-Jalālayn: *Mūsā, we will not endure one sort of food — that is to say, manna and quails. Pray to your Lord for us that He may bring forth for us something of what the earth produces — green herbs, cucumbers, garlic, lentils, onions.*

**Your Lord.**

*Rabbaka.* Not "our Lord." Al-Jalālayn quotes it that way and does not comment, but the pronoun is doing work. They are asking Mūsā to petition a God they address in the second person as his.

**Fūm — and what it means.**

There is a real textual question here, and Ibn Kathīr sets it out:

*As for the fūm, Ibn Masʿūd read it thūm — garlic. Also, Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated that al-Ḥasan said about the verse, "Ibn ʿAbbās said that fūm means garlic." He also said that the expression fumu-lannā means "bake for us," according to the languages of old.*

*Ibn Jarīr commented, "If this is true, then fūm is one of the words whose pronunciation was altered — the letter fāʾ was replaced by the letter thāʾ."*

So: garlic, or wheat, or "bake for us." The sources keep all three.

**Mūsā's answer.**

*Atastabdilūna alladhī huwa adnā bi-lladhī huwa khayr.* Al-Jalālayn gives the grammar and the tone: *Would you exchange what is better — more noble — that is, do you substitute this with what is lowlier? The hamza of a-tastabdilūna is for rebuke.*

An interrogative of rebuke. Not a question. A reproach shaped as one — the same construction as 2:44's *do you preach righteousness and fail to practise it?*

Tanwīr al-Miqbās spells out both sides of the exchange: *Would you exchange that which is higher — i.e. that which is better and more honourable: honey and quails — for that which is lower, that which is much worse: lentils and onions?*

Al-Mukhtaṣar adds what made the manna better, and it is not the taste: *you wanted to exchange manna and quails, which were better and nobler and came to you without effort or work, for what was lesser and worse.*

*Without effort or work.* The manna was not better food. It was free time. That is what Tazkīrul Qurʾān said at verse 60, and it is what they were trading away.

**Go down to any village.**

Al-Jalālayn: *they thus refused to change their mind, and he — Mūsā — supplicated to God, and He said, "Go down to a city, whichever city it may be; you shall have there what you demanded," of vegetable produce.*

Tanwīr al-Miqbās: *Go down to any city — where you came from; and it is also said that this means any city — thus you shall get that which you demand.*

Maʿārif states what the instruction actually was: *Allah commanded them through Sayyidunā Mūsā to go to a certain town which lay somewhere in the wilderness, to till and cultivate the land there, to grow and eat whatever they liked.*

*Cultivate.* The answer to "we want vegetables" was "then farm." Which is the answer to wanting what you can get by working, when you have been given what you cannot get at all.

**Disgrace and misery.**

*Ḍuribat ʿalayhimu adhdhillatu wa al-maskanah.* Al-Jalālayn's gloss is the most vivid in the six sources:

*And abasement, submissiveness and wretchedness — that is, the signs of poverty — on account of their submissiveness and debasement that always accompany them, even if they be rich, in the same way that a coin never changes its mint.*

*Even if they be rich.* Not poverty as a bank balance. A manner.

Tanwīr al-Miqbās reads it legally: *And humiliation — the capitation tax — and wretchedness — the attire of poverty — were stamped upon them, were imposed on them.*

Al-Jalālayn's verb matters: *stamped*. The same word Tanwīr uses. A mint mark.

**And killing the prophets.**

*Wa yaqtulūna an-nabiyyīna bi-ghayri al-ḥaqq.* Maʿārif:

*Even otherwise, it was so usual with them not only to transgress divine commandments but also to deny them outright. They had also been slaying a number of prophets at different times — they knew they were committing a misdeed, but their hostility to the truth and their stubbornness in disobedience made them blind to the nature of their conduct and its consequences.*

*Bi-ghayri al-ḥaqq* — unjustly, without right. Maʿārif's point is that the phrase is not informational. Nobody kills a prophet *with* right. It is there to say that they knew.

**This is a fair reward.**

Ibn Kathīr's summary of the whole verse is the plainest available: *Remember how you asked Mūsā to exchange this type of food for an inferior type that consists of vegetation, and so forth.*

And Maʿārif's closing: *Through such persistent and wilful misdemeanour they drew upon themselves the wrath of Allah. Disgrace and degradation settled upon them forever. That is to say, they no longer had any respect in the eyes of others, nor magnanimity in themselves.*

Tazkīrul Qurʾān gives the last word, and it explains the whole exchange:

*Discontented with the basic necessities of life, they sought to indulge in worldly luxury. So hardened did they become that even clear signs of God could not move their hearts. They opposed and even killed those servants of God who sought to admonish them.*

They asked for onions. The verse answers with disgrace, wrath, and the prophets they killed — because the onions were not about onions. They were about preferring the ordinary to the given, and that preference, pursued far enough, kills prophets.

62.text:
*Indeed, the believers, Jews, Christians, and Sabians — whoever truly believes in Allah and the Last Day and does good will have their reward with their Lord. And there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve.*

**The most contested verse in the sūrah so far.**

Sixty-one verses of the Children of Israel's failures, and then this. The commentators all felt the problem and all answered it, and their answers are not identical.

**Where the verse sits.**

Ibn Kathīr explains the placement:

*After Allah described the condition — and punishment — of those who defy His commands, fall into His prohibitions and transgress set limits by committing prohibited acts, He stated that the earlier nations who were righteous and obedient received the rewards for their good deeds. This shall be the case, until the Day of Judgment.*

Maʿārif gives the pastoral reason, and it is the gentlest reading in the six sources:

*The previous verse spoke of how the Israelites drew upon themselves the wrath of Allah through their habitual insolence and disobedience. Now, this account may lead the listeners, or the Jews themselves, to suppose that, in view of such transgression, their tawbah (repentance), if they agree to offer it, would not be acceptable to Allah. In order to dispel such a misgiving, the present verse lays down a general principle: no matter how a man has been behaving earlier, so long as he submits himself fully to the commandments of Allah in his beliefs and in his deeds both, he is acceptable to Allah, and will get his reward.*

After sixty verses of indictment, a verse saying that the indictment is not permanent.

**The four communities.**

Tazkīrul Qurʾān names all four, and its list is the most informative:

*Four communities are mentioned in this verse: Muslims, who are the followers of the Prophet Muhammad; Jews who follow the Prophet Moses; Christians, who follow the Prophet Jesus; and Sabaeans, who adhered to the teachings of John the Baptist, the Prophet Yaḥyā. The last-mentioned sect resided in Iraq in ancient times, but is now extinct. They were people of the Book, and offered their prayers facing the Kaʿbah in Makkah.*

The other identifications of the Ṣābiʾūn differ. Al-Jalālayn: *a Christian or Jewish sect.* Tanwīr al-Miqbās is the most specific and the strangest: *a Christian sect whose members shave the middle of their heads, read the Gospel, worship the angels, and say, "our hearts have returned (sabaʿat) unto Allah."*

Al-Mukhtaṣar: *said to be a group who followed prophets who were of the faith of Ibrāhīm.*

Note what Tanwīr does with the name. *Ṣābiʾūn* from *sabaʿat* — returned. A community named after its own claim.

**What Tazkīrul makes of the list.**

Its conclusion is the widest statement in the six sources, and it is worth quoting in full:

*Here the Muslims have not been mentioned separately, but have been grouped with other communities associated with prophets. This means that all ethnic groups are equal in the sight of God; no community is inherently superior to any other. Only true belief and righteous actions are rewarded with salvation. This is a rule that applies consistently to every community. No one, whether he calls himself Muslim, Jew, Christian or Sabaean, is exempt from this rule. Belonging to a particular community gives no special status in the eyes of God. God elevates to a high rank only those who have sought to mould their own lives according to His divine scheme.*

*No one is exempt from this rule.* Including Muslims. That is the sharpest edge of the verse, and Tazkīrul is the only one of the six to point at it directly.

**The restriction the others add.**

Ibn Kathīr records the decisive qualification, and it comes from Ibn ʿAbbās:

*ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥah narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās, about "Verily, those who believe and those who are Jews and Christians, and Sabians, whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day," that Allah revealed the following verse afterwards: "And whoever seeks religion other than Islam, it will not be accepted from him, and he is in the Hereafter among the losers" (3:85).*

Al-Mukhtaṣar states it plainly: *This was the case before the Prophet Muhammad was sent. Now his message of Islam — devotion and dedication to Allah — is the only way of life accepted by Allah.*

Al-Jalālayn places the same limit inside the verse itself: *whoever from among them believes in God and the Last Day, in the time of our Prophet, and performs righteous deeds according to the Law given to him.*

*In the time of our Prophet.* The four communities are named, but the condition is tied to the moment of revelation.

**Maʿārif's warning against the loose reading.**

He says it bluntly, in a footnote aimed at his own century:

*Contrary to the flaccid fancies of some "modernizers" who are very happy with themselves over their "liberalism" and "tolerance", the present verse does not open the way to salvation for each and every "man of good will" irrespective of the creed he follows. If one reads the verse in its proper context and along with other relevant verses of the Holy Qurʾān, one will easily see that the verse, in fact, promises [salvation to those who accept Islam].*

**The three conditions.**

Whoever *believes in Allah*, *and the Last Day*, *and does good*. Three things, and the third is a verb.

Al-Jalālayn notes the grammar that ties them to one person: *the singular person of the verbs āmana, "believes," and ʿamila, "performs," takes account of the singular form of man, "whoever" — but in what comes afterwards, of the plural pronouns, its plural meaning is taken into account.*

One person, then many. The verse speaks of a category through an individual.

**Their reward with their Lord.**

Ibn Kathīr supplies the two verses that complete the promise:

*Therefore, whoever follows the unlettered Messenger and Prophet shall acquire eternal happiness, and shall neither fear from what will happen in the future nor become sad for what has been lost in the past. Similarly, Allah said, "No doubt! Verily, the awliyāʾ of Allah, no fear shall come upon them nor shall they grieve" (10:62).*

*The angels will proclaim to the dying believers, as mentioned: "Verily, those who say, 'Our Lord is Allah (alone),' and then they stand firm, on them the angels will descend (at the time of their death), saying, 'Fear not, nor grieve! But receive the glad tidings of Paradise which you have been promised!'" (41:30).*

Tanwīr al-Miqbās offers a third reading of the phrase: *It is also said that this means: they shall have no fear when death is slain and hell is closed.*

No fear forward, no grief backward. The two directions in which a person can be undone, both closed.

**What the verse is doing in the address.**

The address to the Children of Israel has run twenty-three verses. Verse 61 ended with wrath and disgrace stamped on them. Verse 62 then opens the door, and every one of the six commentators is at pains to say how far it opens.

Tazkīrul reads it as universal. Maʿārif reads it as a guarantee that repentance still works. Ibn Kathīr, Al-Mukhtaṣar and Al-Jalālayn read it as true and bounded by 3:85.

They are all reading the same verse. The disagreement is about how the bound is drawn, not about whether the promise is real.

And the promise is real. Verse 63 goes straight back to the mountain.

63.text:
*And remember when We took a covenant from you and raised the mountain above you, saying, "Hold firmly to that Scripture which We have given you and observe its teachings so perhaps you will become mindful of Allah."*

**The mountain raised over a people.**

This is the sūrah's most extraordinary image, and it is stated in a single clause.

Al-Jalālayn: *And mention when We made a covenant with you — your pledge to act according to what is in the Torah — and We had raised above you the Mount, which We uprooted from the earth and placed above you when you refused to accept it, that is, the Torah.*

Tanwīr al-Miqbās: *And when We made a covenant with you — took your consent — and caused the Mount to tower above you: pulled out and fixed high above your heads the mountain, for taking the covenant.*

Ibn Kathīr supplies the fuller Qurʾānic account from sūrah 7: *And remember when We raised the mountain over them as if it had been a canopy, and they thought that it was going to fall on them.*

*A canopy.* The mountain as a roof they could look up at.

**Which mountain.**

Ibn Kathīr settles it with the full list of authorities:

*The mount mentioned here is aṭ-Ṭūr, just as it was explained in sūrat al-Aʿrāf, according to the tafsīr of Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, ʿAṭāʾ, ʿIkrimah, al-Ḥasan, aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk, ar-Rabīʿ ibn Anas and others. This is more obvious.*

Then a curiosity about the name: *There is another report from Ibn ʿAbbās saying, "The Ṭūr is a type of mountain that vegetation grows on; if no vegetation grows on it, it is not called Ṭūr."*

So the word itself carries green.

And Ibn ʿAbbās in the ḥadīth of trials: *"When they — the Jews — refused to obey, Allah raised the mountain above their heads so that they would listen."*

*So that they would listen.* Not to crush them. To be heard.

**Maʿārif's full account of how it came to this.**

He tells the whole story, and it is the only connected version in the six sources:

*Having received the Torah from Allah, Sayyidunā Mūsā returned from Mount Ṭūr (Sinai) and recited it to the Israelites. The injunctions contained in the Book were rather rigorous, but their conduct and habits of mind really called for such strict discipline.*

*To begin with, they replied that they would not obey the injunctions until and unless Allah Himself told them that it was His book. Seventy men, as we have related above, were selected to go to Mount Ṭūr and to hear Allah attest the authenticity of the Torah.*

This is the seventy from verse 55 — the men struck by the thunderbolt. They wanted proof, and they got it, and verse 56 says they were brought back to life.

*On their return, they bore witness to the Torah being a Book of Allah, but added something on their own to what Allah had actually said. For, they told the Israelites that Allah had allowed them to act upon the injunctions only as much as they could, and had promised to forgive them for what they could not accomplish.*

They went to hear God, heard Him, came back, and edited. That is verse 59's failure again — the changed word — at the scale of a covenant.

*They had always and instinctively been prone to rebellion against Allah; then, the injunctions were, no doubt, stern; and now they got a new pretext for being negligent. So, the Israelites flatly refused to obey the injunctions, insisting that it was beyond their endurance to act upon such harsh regulations.*

*In reply to this insolence, Allah commanded the angels to raise Mount Ṭūr and let it hang in the air above their heads, as a threat that if they did not fulfil their covenant with Allah, it would fall on them and crush them. The Israelites, then, had no choice but to submit.*

*The angels.* And *had no choice but to submit.* Which is the problem Maʿārif then raises.

**The question the verse invites.**

Maʿārif continues: *A doubt is quite likely to arise here* — the doubt being whether a covenant extracted under a hanging mountain is a covenant at all.

He does not dismiss it. He records it as a real question, which is itself worth noting: the tradition keeps the uncomfortable reading.

The answer the sources converge on is that the mountain did not create the obligation. The Torah did. The mountain made them look at it.

**Hold firmly.**

*Khudhū mā ātaynākum bi-quwwah.* Ibn Kathīr collects the glosses:

*Al-Ḥasan said that Allah's statement, "Hold fast to that which We have given you," means the Tawrāh. Mujāhid said that the verse commanded, "Strictly adhere to it." Abū al-ʿĀliyah and ar-Rabīʿ said that "and remember that which is therein" [means to act upon it].*

Al-Jalālayn: *and We said, "Take forcefully — seriously and with effort — what We have given you, and remember what is in it, acting in accordance with it, so that you might preserve yourselves" from the Fire, or acts of disobedience.*

Tanwīr al-Miqbās: *Hold fast that which We have given you — comply with what We have given of the scripture in earnestness and diligence, and remember that which is therein of reward and chastisement, and recollect what is in it of the lawful and unlawful.*

Al-Mukhtaṣar: *take what He had revealed to you of the Torah seriously and carefully, not taking it for granted or being lazy about it.*

*Bi-quwwah* — with strength. Not with enthusiasm. With effort.

**So perhaps you will become mindful.**

*Laʿallakum tattaqūn.* Tanwīr al-Miqbās: *that ye may ward off evil — in order that you may ward off Allah's wrath and torment, and so that you may obey Him.*

Al-Jalālayn: *so that you might preserve yourselves from the Fire.*

Taqwā as the stated purpose of the whole arrangement — the covenant, the Torah, and the mountain. Not obedience for its own sake. Awareness.

**What Tazkīrul makes of it.**

Tazkīrul Qurʾān turns the episode into the general rule of faith, and it is the most striking comment on the verse:

*A covenant was made with Moses' people that they would faithfully carry out the divine teachings given to them in the form of the Ten Commandments. The Talmud tells how, at this time, God turned a mountain upside down, holding it above them and told them either to accept the teachings of the Torah, or be destroyed there and then.*

Then the turn: *The same is the case with everyone who embraces true faith. To have faith is to make a contract with God that one will live and die in accordance with His will. What a grave pledge this is. On the one hand there is man — a tiny, helpless speck in God's world — and on the other, God, whose might upholds the universe.*

*Everyone who believes in God should go through the same experience as Moses' people. Everyone who binds himself to the contract of faith should live in the fear of breaking his religious vows.*

The mountain is not an exception in the story. It is the visible form of something every believer signs.

**Why the verse is a favour.**

It sits in the list of favours, and the mountain sounds like a threat. But Ibn Kathīr's framing is that Allah *reminded the Children of Israel of the pledges, covenants and promises that He took from them to believe in Him alone, without a partner, and follow His Messengers.*

Being given a covenant is the favour. Being made to see its weight was the mercy inside it. Verse 64 says what they did next.

64.text:
*Yet you turned away afterwards. Had it not been for Allah's grace and mercy upon you, you would have certainly been of the losers.*

**Four words after the mountain.**

Verse 63 raised a mountain over them. Verse 64 is eleven words long in Arabic and says they walked away from it anyway.

Al-Jalālayn's comment on the verse is the shortest in his entire tafsīr of this passage, and he flags it himself:

*Then you turned away thereafter — and but for God's bounty and His mercy towards you, you would have been among the losers. There is no commentary on this verse.*

*There is no commentary on this verse.* After the mountain, the exegete has nothing to add. The verse needs no explanation.

Tanwīr al-Miqbās: *Then, even after that, you turned away — you turned your back on the covenant.*

*Even after that.* The phrase carries the whole weight.

**What "turned away" costs.**

Al-Mukhtaṣar: *Yet after making a firm promise, you broke the contract and rebelled. If it had not been for Allah's favour in His tolerance towards you, and His mercy, accepting when you asked for forgiveness, then you would be among the losers because of your turning away and rebellion.*

Maʿārif states the scale of what was deserved:

*The Israelites went against the covenant they had made with Allah. The sin was so grave that one could have expected utter destruction and ruin to descend on them as a punishment. But Allah, in His mercy, spared them in so far as physical life is concerned, although they will have to pay for their treason in the other world.*

*Spare them in so far as physical life is concerned.* They were not destroyed. The bill was deferred, not cancelled.

**Two kinds of mercy.**

Maʿārif then makes a distinction that the verse depends on:

*Allah's mercy is of two kinds. One is general and extends to believers and disbelievers alike — its action is to be seen in the shape of worldly well-being and prosperity. The other is special, and pertains to believers alone — it will manifest itself particularly in the other world in the shape of salvation and closeness to Allah.*

The verse names both: *faḍl* — grace, bounty — and *raḥmah*, mercy. On Maʿārif's reading the first is the general mercy and the second the special one. They survived by the first. The second is what verse 62 had just promised.

**Who the verse is addressed to.**

Maʿārif makes a point that explains why this is in an address to the present:

*It appears that the last phrase of the present verse has been addressed to the Jews who were the contemporaries of the Holy Prophet. Since having faith in him is also a part of the covenant, these Jews too have been included among those who had been guilty of infringement.*

The covenant at Sinai included believing in the messengers who would come. So the audience in Madinah is inside it.

*In this verse, Allah asks them to realize that it is in His mercy alone that He has not, in spite of their treason, sent down on them the kind of catastrophic punishment in this world as used to descend on the other infidels and traitors who have gone before.*

**The mercy identified.**

Tanwīr al-Miqbās names it: *and if it had not been for the grace of Allah upon you, by deferring His punishment, and His mercy, by sending Muhammad to you.*

Maʿārif records the same reading with its evidence:

*Since a number of authentic aḥādīth declare that it is the barakah of the Holy Prophet that catastrophic punishments no longer descend on any people, some commentators have identified this particular mercy and grace of Allah with the sending down of Muhammad as a Prophet and Messenger of Allah.*

The mercy that spared them is, on this reading, the Prophet standing in front of them. The address to the Children of Israel is being delivered through the very mercy it describes.

**You would have been among the losers.**

*Lakuntum mina al-khāsirīn.* Al-Mukhtaṣar: *you would be among the losers.* Tanwīr al-Miqbās expands: *you would have been among the duped, who are exposed to Allah's punishment.*

*Khāsir* — one who has made a losing transaction. The sūrah has used the word repeatedly: 2:16 *their trade brought no profit*, 2:27 *the losers*, and now here. The same vocabulary throughout.

**The verse's position in the address.**

It is the shortest of the covenant verses and the most damning. Verse 63 gave them a book and a mountain. Verse 64 says they left. And it says the only reason they were still alive to be addressed was a mercy they were not entitled to.

The address has now covered the exodus, the calf, the seventy men, the wilderness, the city, the plague, the springs, the food — and at every one, the same two-beat rhythm. A favour. A turning away.

Verse 65 moves to a new story, and it is the worst one yet.

65.text:
*You are already aware of those of you who broke the Sabbath. We said to them, "Be disgraced apes!"*

**A verse about fishing.**

Two verses, fourteen words in English translation, describing people turned into apes for catching fish on the wrong day. It is the sūrah's most startling punishment, and the commentators take the mechanism apart carefully.

**You already know.**

The verse opens by telling them they know this story. Ibn Kathīr: *This verse means, O Jews! Remember that Allah sent His torment on the village that disobeyed Him and broke their pledge and their covenant to observe the sanctity of the Sabbath.*

Tanwīr al-Miqbās: *And ye know — you indeed know and heard about the punishment of those of you who broke the Sabbath.*

Al-Jalālayn notes the grammar: *And verily — wa-la-qad, the lām is for oaths — you know that there were those among you who transgressed, violated the Sabbath by fishing when We had forbidden you to do so. These were the inhabitants of Aylah.*

Aylah — modern ʿAqabah, on the Red Sea. A named town.

Tanwīr al-Miqbās dates it: *and this at the time of Dāwūd.* Maʿārif agrees: *This episode belongs to the time of Sayyidunā Dāwūd (David).*

**What the Sabbath was.**

Maʿārif explains the rule: *Allah had appointed Saturday as the sabt, or the sacred day, for the Israelites; it was specially set apart for prayers and worship, and hence fishing was prohibited on this day. But these people lived on the sea-shore, and were very fond of fish.*

*They lived on the sea-shore.* The prohibition fell on the one thing their whole economy was built on. And sūrah 7 supplies the detail: *when their fish came to them openly on the Sabbath day, and did not come to them on the day they had no Sabbath. Thus We made a trial of them.*

The fish came on Saturday. Not by chance — *thus We made a trial of them.* The prohibition and the temptation arrived together, on purpose.

**The trick.**

This is the heart of the verse, and Ibn Kathīr describes it precisely:

*They began using deceitful means to avoid honoring the Sabbath, by placing nets, ropes and artificial pools of water for the purpose of fishing before the Sabbath. When the fish came in abundance on Saturday as usual, they were caught in the ropes and nets for the rest of Saturday. During the night, the Jews collected the fish after the Sabbath ended.*

Nothing was done on Saturday. The nets were set Friday. The fish were collected Saturday night. Every step fell outside the prohibited day.

Al-Mukhtaṣar: *who prepared to fish on the Sabbath when they were not allowed to do so, and did so through trickery. They set up nets in preparation for the Sabbath.*

Maʿārif records the escalation: *Al-Qurṭubī says that the Israelites, at first, invented all sorts of clever pretences for catching fish on Saturday, and gradually started doing so openly.*

First the loophole. Then the open breach. That is the shape of the story.

**Why the punishment fit.**

Ibn Kathīr gives the reasoning, and it is the best sentence in the passage:

*When they did that, Allah changed them from humans into monkeys, the animals having the form closest to humans. Their evil deeds and deceit appeared lawful on the surface, but they were in reality wicked. This is why their punishment was compatible with their crime.*

*Appeared lawful on the surface, but they were in reality wicked.* They kept the letter of the law perfectly. And they were turned into the animal that looks most like a human being and is not one — the punishment matching the crime in form.

**The division in the town.**

Maʿārif tells the rest, and it is the part verse 66 picks up:

*There now grew a division amongst them on this point. On the one hand were these transgressors, and, on the other, some scholars and pious men who tried to dissuade them from such disobedience. When the former paid no heed to them, the latter broke away altogether from the sinners, and began to live in a separate part of the town.*

*One day they felt no sound was coming from the other part of the town. Growing curious, they went there and found that all the transgressors had been changed into apes.*

A town gone quiet. That is how the neighbours found out.

*Qaṭādah says that the young ones had become apes, and the old ones swine.*

Ibn ʿAbbās, in the report al-ʿAwfī carried to Ibn Kathīr: *"Allah changed their bodies into those of monkeys and swines."*

**What happened after.**

Maʿārif's account does not stop at the transformation:

*The apes could recognize their relatives and friends, and would approach them weeping out of remorse, and seeking their sympathy and help. Then all of them died after three days.*

Al-Jalālayn confirms the timescale: *and We said to them, "Be apes, despised!" — rejected — and they became so. They died three days later.*

*Could recognize their relatives.* They were not animals that had once been people. They were people who had become animals, still knowing who they were.

Maʿārif then closes a question people ask: *As to the question whether the apes and the swine we see today bear any kinship to these Israelites who had been metamorphosed, the correct position is that people who have been metamorphosed into beasts by Allah as a punishment cease to breed, and leave no progeny.*

No descendants. The line ended in three days.

**Why this verse is in the address.**

It is the sūrah's clearest statement about what obedience is. Not the appearance of keeping a rule. The seventy men who edited the Torah, the people who entered the gate dragging themselves, the people who changed one word — and now a town that kept every technical requirement of the Sabbath and lost the lot.

Tazkīrul Qurʾān says it directly: *Sometimes those entrusted with the law of God go astray by contradicting it in practice, while finding words to make it appear that they are following it to the letter.*

*To the letter.* That is the verse's whole subject.

66.text:
*So We made their fate an example to present and future generations, and a lesson to the God-fearing.*

**The verse that says what the story is for.**

Verse 65 told what happened. Verse 66 says why it is still being told — and it names three audiences.

**Three audiences, in three phrases.**

*Fa-jaʿalnāhā nakālan limā bayna yadayhā wa mā khalfahā wa mawʿiẓatan li-l-muttaqīn.*

Al-Jalālayn parses them: *And We made it — this punishment — an exemplary punishment, a lesson to dissuade others from doing what they did; for all the former times and for the latter — that is, for the people of that time, or those that came later; and an admonition to such as who fear God.*

Al-Mukhtaṣar: *Allah made this village, which had transgressed the limits, an example to the surrounding villages, and an example to those who came after it, so that they would not do the same and deserve the same fate.*

Tanwīr al-Miqbās: *And We made it — turning them into apes — an example — we subjected them to a chastisement — to their own, for the sins they had committed before, and made them a lesson to succeeding generations, in order that they do not follow their example.*

**Nakāl — what the word means.**

Al-Jalālayn glosses it as *an exemplary punishment, a lesson to dissuade others from doing what they did.* Not merely a penalty. A penalty designed to be seen.

The word carries both halves at once: punishment, and the deterrent effect of the punishment being known.

**Why the God-fearing are named separately.**

Al-Jalālayn answers, and it is the sharpest line in the six sources:

*And an admonition to such as who fear God — these are singled out for mention here because they, in contrast to others, are the ones who benefit thereby.*

*Because they are the ones who benefit.* The story is addressed to everyone and lands on some. Al-Jalālayn says plainly that it only lands on the muttaqūn.

Al-Mukhtaṣar defines them: *He made it a reminder for those mindful of Allah, who are careful of facing the consequences of their actions in the life to come, and are mindful of Allah's repayment for those who transgress the limits.*

*Those who are careful of facing the consequences.* Not those who are afraid. Those who count what things will cost.

Tanwīr al-Miqbās names the audience concretely: *and admonition to the God-fearing — and a counsel and warning to those who fear Allah, i.e. Muhammad and his Companions.*

The story about a town on the Red Sea, addressed to Madinah.

**Ibn Kathīr on the structure.**

He ties verses 65 and 66 together with the sūrah's running theme:

*Allah said, "And indeed you knew." This verse means, O Jews! Remember that Allah sent His torment on the village that disobeyed Him and broke their pledge and their covenant to observe the sanctity of the Sabbath.*

*Their pledge and their covenant.* Not a rule they happened to have. Verse 63's covenant, broken at Aylah.

**Maʿārif on the three groups.**

He reads the verse through the division inside the town:

The transgressors became apes. The scholars who separated themselves were spared. And verse 66 says the story was made *an example to present and future generations, and a lesson to the God-fearing.*

The third group — the ones who warned, then withdrew — are the muttaqūn the verse is addressed to. The story is told to the people who did the right thing and found it did not save their neighbours.

**Why the story was preserved at all.**

Three days and they were dead. No progeny. No descendants. By every ordinary measure the punishment was complete and the line ended.

But verse 66 says the real consequence was not the three days. It was that the story would still be read in Madinah fourteen centuries later, and would be read again.

*Nakālan limā bayna yadayhā wa mā khalfahā.* An example to what is before it and what is behind it. The punishment outlived the punished.

**What Tazkīrul makes of it.**

Its reading connects the verse back to the covenant at verse 63 and closes the sequence:

*The Israelites, for instance, were commanded to keep holy the Sabbath day, and refrain from worldly pursuits on that day. But they violated it and went about their work on the Sabbath as on any other day. Furthermore, they sought to justify their actions.*

*Sought to justify their actions.* That is the addition. Not just breaking the rule, but building an argument for it.

**The verse's place.**

Verses 63 to 66 form a single unit: a covenant given with a mountain over their heads, a turning away, and a town that kept the letter of the covenant perfectly and was destroyed for it.

And verse 66 says the destruction was not the end of it. It was the beginning of the story's work — an example, a lesson, an admonition, still being read.

That is what the sūrah has been doing since verse 40. Every verse about the Children of Israel is being told to somebody else.

67.text:
*And remember when Moses said to his people, "Allah commands you to sacrifice a cow." They replied, "Are you mocking us?" Moses responded, "I seek refuge in Allah from acting foolishly!"*

**The verse that names the sūrah.**

Sūrat al-Baqarah — the Cow. Two hundred and eighty-six verses, and the one that gives it its title is a command to slaughter an animal, answered with an accusation of mockery.

**What nobody has told you yet: there was a murder.**

The verse says nothing about it. Al-Jalālayn supplies it in a single clause:

*And mention when Mūsā said to his people — when one among them was killed and the killer was not known, and so they asked Mūsā to pray to God to reveal the killer, which he did: "God commands you to sacrifice a cow."*

Ibn Kathīr records the fullest account, from ʿUbaydah as-Salmānī:

*There was a man from among the Children of Israel who was impotent. He had substantial wealth, and only a nephew who would inherit from him. So his nephew killed him and moved his body at night, placing it at the doorstep of a certain man. The next morning, the nephew cried out for revenge, and the people took up their weapons and almost fought each other.*

*The wise men among them said, "Why would you kill each other, while the Messenger of Allah is still among you?" So they went to Mūsā and mentioned the matter to him.*

A rich man. One heir. A body moved in the night to frame a neighbour. And a town on the point of civil war over it.

**Maʿārif's variant, and what it implies.**

He gives a different version and then draws a chronological conclusion from it:

*According to Mirqāt, a commentary on Mishkāt, a man among the Israelites wanted to marry a girl, but her father refused. The suitor was so incensed that he killed the father, and disappeared.*

*It is mentioned in Maʿālim at-Tanzīl, which says on the authority of al-Kalbī, that Allah had not yet sent down any injunction with regard to manslaughter. If it was so, this shows that the incident happened before the Torah was revealed.*

Two motives in two accounts — inheritance in one, a refused marriage in the other. Both are murders by someone close. Maʿārif keeps both and notes what the second one implies about when this happened.

*Anyhow, the Israelites requested Sayyidunā Mūsā to tell them how to trace the culprit. Under the commandment of Allah, he asked them to sacrifice a cow.*

**Why a cow.**

No source explains the mechanism here. Verse 73 will — the dead man is struck with a piece of the cow and stands up to name his killer. Verse 67 gives only the command, with no reason attached.

Ibn Kathīr states the purpose from Allah's side: *Remember how I blessed you with the miracle of the cow that was the means for discovering the identity of the murderer, when the murdered man was brought back to life.*

The blessing is not the cow. It is what the cow was for.

**"Are you mocking us?"**

*Atattakhidhunā huzuʾā.* The response to a divine command, delivered through their prophet, is an accusation of mockery.

Al-Jalālayn: *They said, "Do you take us in mockery?" — that is, making fun of us when you answer us like this?*

*When you answer us like this.* They asked who killed a man. They were told to slaughter a cow. The answer did not match the question, and they concluded the question had been treated as a joke.

Tanwīr al-Miqbās: *they said: Dost thou make game of us? — are you really mocking us?*

Al-Mukhtaṣar frames it as character: *Instead of hurrying to do so, they said, stubbornly, "Are you making fun of us?"*

**A town about to fight itself.**

Ibn Kathir's account has a detail worth pausing on. The body was placed at a certain man's doorstep, and by morning the whole town had armed.

*The people took up their weapons and almost fought each other.*

Not a family dispute. A community on the edge of killing over a killing. And the people who stopped it were not the elders or the judges - it was *the wise men among them*, whose argument was practical: *Why would you kill each other, while the Messenger of Allah is still among you?*

There is a prophet in the town. Ask him. That single sentence is what brings the whole narrative to Mūsā, and it is why the command that follows arrives with no explanation attached - it is an answer to a question that was asked in a moment of near-civil-war.

**Mūsā's answer.**

*Aʿūdhu bi-llāhi an akūna mina al-jāhilīn.* He does not defend the command. He does not explain it. He takes refuge.

Tanwīr al-Miqbās: *He — Mūsā — answered: Allah forbid that I should be among the foolish! God forbid that I ever mock the believers.*

Al-Jalālayn: *He said, "I take refuge with — I seek defence with — God, lest I should be one of the ignorant," one of those who indulge in mockery.*

Al-Mukhtaṣar expands what the refuge covers: *Mūsā replied that he asked for Allah's protection from being one of the ignorant people, who lied about Allah, and made fun of other people.*

Two things a prophet must not be: a liar about God, and a mocker of people. Mūsā names both and takes refuge from both.

**Why this verse sits here.**

Verses 40 to 66 have been a list. Favour after favour, each followed by a failure — the calf, the seventy men, the changed word, the onions, the mountain, the Sabbath. Every failure had a shape: they were given something clear and made it complicated.

Verse 67 begins the sūrah's namesake story, and it is the same shape at its purest. *Slaughter a cow.* Three words. And the answer is that Mūsā is joking.

Ibn Kathīr's summary of the whole narrative says what it cost:

*Had they not disputed, it would have been sufficient for them to slaughter any cow. However, they disputed, and the matter was made more difficult for them, until they ended up looking for the specific cow that they were later ordered to slaughter.*

Any cow. That was the command. Verses 68 to 71 are them talking their way out of it.

68.text:
*They said, "Call upon your Lord to clarify for us what type of cow it should be!" He replied, "Allah says, 'The cow should neither be old nor young but in between. So do as you are commanded!'"*

**The first of three questions.**

They had been told to slaughter a cow. Any cow. And the first thing they did was ask for specifications.

Al-Jalālayn marks the moment they stopped doubting: *But when they realised that he was being serious, they said, "Pray to your Lord for us that He may make clear to us what she may be" — its true nature.*

*When they realised that he was being serious.* Verse 67's mockery had been a test of whether he meant it. He did. And instead of obeying, they began negotiating the terms.

Tanwīr al-Miqbās puts the question concretely: *They said: Pray for us unto your Lord that He make clear to us what she is — whether the cow is large or small.*

**Your Lord.**

*Rabbaka* again, as in verse 61 with the onions. Not "our Lord."

They are asking Mūsā to petition on their behalf, and the pronoun is the sūrah's quiet record of the distance. Ibn Kathīr gives the sense: *"Call upon your Lord for us that He may make plain to us what it is!" — meaning, "What is this cow and what is its description?"*

**Neither old nor young.**

*Lā fāriḍun wa lā bikr.* Ibn Kathīr collects the glosses, and the list of authorities is the longest in this passage:

*Neither too old nor too young — meaning, that it is neither old nor below the age of breeding. This is the opinion of Abū al-ʿĀliyah, As-Suddī, Mujāhid, ʿIkrimah, ʿAṭiyyah al-ʿAwfī, ʿAṭāʾ al-Khurāsānī, Wahb ibn Munabbih, aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk, al-Ḥasan, Qatādah and Ibn ʿAbbās.*

Eleven authorities on one phrase. Al-Jalālayn renders it: *she is a cow neither old nor virgin — that is, young — middling between the two in terms of age.*

*Neither old nor virgin.* Bikr — a heifer that has not calved.

**In between.**

*ʿAwānun bayna dhālik.* Aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk's report from Ibn ʿAbbās gives the reason for the middle: *"Neither old nor young. Rather, she was at the age when the cow is strongest and fittest."*

Not an arbitrary midpoint. The prime of the animal's life.

Tanwīr al-Miqbās reads it as size instead of age: *between the two conditions — neither large nor small.* The two readings, age and size, sit side by side in the sources without resolution.

Al-Mukhtaṣar: *Mūsā told them that Allah said that it was neither old nor young, but was between the two.*

**So do as you are commanded.**

The verse's second half is the part that gets skipped, and it is where the rebuke lives.

Tanwīr al-Miqbās: *so do that which ye are commanded — and ask no further questions.*

*And ask no further questions.* The gloss supplies what the verse implies. Mūsā answers the question and then tells them to stop asking.

Al-Jalālayn: *so do what you have been commanded — by way of sacrificing it.*

Al-Mukhtaṣar: *and he told them to do what Allah had instructed them to.*

Three sources, three renderings, and all of them end on the imperative. The question was answered. The instruction stands.

**What the question cost them.**

Maʿārif's summary of the whole passage is the clearest statement of its meaning:

*These verses show how the Israelites were disposed to disobedience, and how this inclination expressed itself in different forms. The ḥadīth says that if these people had obeyed Allah's commandment without raising so many doubts and asking unnecessary questions, such strict condition would not have been imposed on them, and the sacrifice of any cow whatsoever would have been accepted.*

*Such strict condition would not have been imposed on them.* The specifications were not in the original command. Every one of them is a consequence of asking.

Ibn Kathīr says the same from Ibn ʿAbbās and ʿUbaydah: *Had they slaughtered a cow, any cow, it would have been sufficient for them. Instead, they made the matter difficult, and this is why Allah made it even more difficult for them.*

**What the answer did not do.**

Notice what is missing. Mūsā answers the question fully - neither old nor young, in between, at the age when the cow is strongest. That is a complete answer.

It does not narrow the field enough to find one cow. A middling-aged cow is the most common animal in any herd. If the specification had been intended to identify a particular animal, it would have done so.

This is the shape of the whole passage, and it is easy to miss: every answer is accurate and none of them is sufficient. The insufficiency is not in the answer. It is in the question. They had asked what the cow should be, and the answer told them what it should be.

Had they gone out and brought back any middling-aged cow, the story would have ended at verse 68.

**Why this verse matters beyond the story.**

Tazkīrul Qurʾān draws the general rule, and it is the sharpest comment on the passage:

*Another mistake that the Israelites had made was to destroy the simplicity of divine religion by involving themselves in complicated theological wrangling. They had to learn to interpret God's will in a straightforward manner and obey it immediately.
