This was another lesson that was taught under the pretext of this murder case: hair-splitting to define the exact scope of divine edicts will only make things difficult for everyone; additional conditions will only complicate the carrying out of what had originally been a simple commandment.*

*Hair-splitting to define the exact scope of divine edicts.* That is verse 68 in one phrase. They asked what the cow should be, and the answer made the cow harder to find.

And there were two more questions coming.

69.text:
*They said, "Call upon your Lord to specify for us its colour." He replied, "Allah says, 'It should be a bright yellow cow—pleasant to see.'"*

**The second question.**

They had their answer about age. Instead of going to find a middling-aged cow, they asked about its colour.

Al-Jalālayn: *They said, "Pray to your Lord for us that He make clear to us what her colour may be."*

Tanwīr al-Miqbās: *They said: Pray for us unto your Lord that He make clear to us of what colour she is.*

The same formulation as verse 68 — *call upon your Lord* — with a new specification attached.

**A yellow cow.**

*Ṣafrāʾ fāqiʿun lawnuhā.*

Al-Jalālayn: *He said, "He says, she shall be a golden cow, bright in colour" — that is, of a very intense yellow — "gladdening to beholders," its beauty will please those that look at it.*

Al-Mukhtaṣar: *Mūsā told them that Allah said that it was a yellow cow, with a very strong colour, which was pleasing to everyone who saw it.*

*Very strong colour.* Fāqiʿ — saturated, intense. Not pale yellow. The word means a yellow that has weight to it.

**Two readings of fāqiʿ.**

Ibn Kathīr records a variant from Ibn ʿAbbās that points the other way:

*In his tafsīr, al-ʿAwfī reported from Ibn ʿAbbās that "bright in its colour" means "a deep yellowish white."*

Intense yellow, or deep yellowish white. The same phrase, two reports, and Ibn Kathīr keeps both.

**And a third reading of the cow entirely.**

Tanwīr al-Miqbās gives a description that contradicts both:

*Lo! He saith: Surely she is a yellow cow — her hoofs and horns are yellow while her body is black. Bright is her colour — her colour is light, gladdening beholders — pleasing those who look at her.*

*Her body is black.* Yellow hooves and horns on a black cow, with a bright colour. It is not reconcilable with a wholly yellow cow, and the sources do not try to reconcile it.

Three descriptions in three sources. The verse says *a bright yellow cow*, and the commentators fill in around it differently.

**Pleasant to see.**

*Tasurru an-nāẓirīn.* As-Suddī, recorded by Ibn Kathīr, gives the plain gloss: *meaning, that it pleases those who see it.*

Al-Mukhtaṣar: *pleasing to everyone who saw it.*

This is the only aesthetic description of anything in the whole address to the Children of Israel. After the calf, the plague, the apes, the mountain — a cow that was beautiful.

And that detail is what made it expensive. Verse 71 will say they paid its weight in gold for it.

**What the question added.**

Verse 68 narrowed the age. Verse 69 narrows the colour. Each question removes cows from the field.

Tazkīrul Qurʾān's rule covers this exactly: *hair-splitting to define the exact scope of divine edicts will only make things difficult for everyone; additional conditions will only complicate the carrying out of what had originally been a simple commandment.*

They asked for a colour. They got one — the hardest colour to find in a herd.

Maʿārif's ḥadīth is the summary: *if these people had obeyed Allah's commandment without raising so many doubts and asking unnecessary questions, such strict condition would not have been imposed on them, and the sacrifice of any cow whatsoever would have been accepted.*

Any cow. Still available to them at this point, technically. They ask one more time.

70.text:
*Again they said, "Call upon your Lord so that He may make clear to us which cow, for all cows look the same to us. Then, Allah willing, we will be guided to the right one."*

**The third question — and the only time they say "if Allah wills."**

Two questions in, and they ask a third. This verse is the shortest of the three and carries the sūrah's most quoted line.

**The question.**

Al-Jalālayn parses it, and notes that it is a different question from the first two:

*They said, "Pray to your Lord for us that He make clear to us what she may be — does it graze freely or is it used in labour?; the cows — that is, the species described in the way mentioned — are all alike to us, because there are many of them and we have not been able to find the one sought after; and if God wills we shall then be guided" to it.*

Tanwīr al-Miqbās: *They said: pray for us unto your Lord that He make clear to us what cow she is — whether she ploughs the soil or not. Lo! Cows are much alike to us — we cannot distinguish much between cows.*

Al-Mukhtaṣar: *They continued in their stubbornness, telling Mūsā to ask Allah to further clarify the nature of the cow. They said that there were many cows fitting the description, and they could not therefore identify it.*

*Many cows fitting the description.* By now the age and the colour have narrowed nothing enough. They are asking for the thing that distinguishes one from another.

**Their reason.**

And it sounds reasonable. That is the difficulty of the verse. Three questions, and the third one is: *there are too many cows that match, tell us which.*

Al-Jalālayn's gloss makes the reasoning explicit: *because there are many of them and we have not been able to find the one sought after.*

They are not refusing. They are explaining why they cannot comply.

**Then, Allah willing.**

*Wa innā in shāʾa Llāhu la-muhtadūn.* After two verses of *call upon your Lord*, they add the proviso.

Al-Jalālayn records the ḥadīth about it, and it is the most striking line in the passage:

*In one ḥadīth it is reported: "Had they not uttered the proviso in shāʾa Llāh, it would never have been made clear to them."*

*It would never have been made clear.* Not to them. At all.

The two prior questions had produced specifications that made the task harder. The third produced a condition — and the ḥadīth says the condition was only answered because of the proviso.

**Why the proviso matters.**

Every specification before this had been a narrowing. This one is different in kind: they are not asking what the cow is like. They are asking which cow it is.

And they attach *in shāʾa Llāh* to their own guidance — *we will be guided*. Not "we will do it." Not "we will obey." *We will be guided.*

Al-Mukhtaṣar records how it ends: *insisting that they would then, if Allah willed, be guided to the right cow for sacrifice.*

Tanwīr al-Miqbās offers a second reading of what "guided" means here: *and lo! If Allah wills, we may be led rightfully — to its fitting description; as it is said that this means: we may be led to the murder of ʿĀmil.*

*To the murder of ʿĀmil.* The name of the killer, in one report. On that reading they are saying: if Allah wills, we will find out who did it — which is what they came to Mūsā for in the first place.

**Why the third question is the hardest to fault.**

Read the three questions in order. Verse 68: what type. Verse 69: what colour. Verse 70: which one.

The first two are questions about a category. The third is a question about identity, and it has a reason attached that sounds entirely fair - there are too many cows that match, we cannot pick.

That is what makes verse 70 the sūrah's quiet diagnosis. The first two questions were stalling. The third is the one a reasonable person asks. And it is the one that costs them a skin's weight in gold.

Al-Jalālayn's phrasing keeps the reason visible rather than dismissing it: *because there are many of them and we have not been able to find the one sought after.* The commentators do not call this question dishonest. They call it the third one.

**Maʿārif on the pattern.**

He groups verses 68 to 71 together and states what they show:

*These verses show how the Israelites were disposed to disobedience, and how this inclination expressed itself in different forms.*

*In different forms.* Verse 67 was mockery. Verses 68 and 69 were questions. Verse 70 is a question with a pious formula attached. The disobedience does not disappear — it changes register.

**The verse's place in the pattern.**

Ibn Kathīr's frame for the whole passage: *Allah mentioned the stubbornness of the Children of Israel and the many unnecessary questions they asked their Messengers. This is why when they were stubborn, Allah made the decisions difficult for them.*

*Made the decisions difficult for them.* Not as arbitrary severity. As the direct consequence.

And verse 70 is the hinge. It is the last question, and it carries the proviso that unlocks the answer. Verse 71 gives the description — and the price.

71.text:
*He replied, "Allah says, 'It should have been used neither to till the soil nor water the fields; wholesome and without blemish.'" They said, "Now you have come with the truth." Yet they still slaughtered it hesitantly.*

**The description, and what it did.**

Verse 71 gives the last specification — and it is the one that makes the cow nearly impossible to find.

**Unyoked.**

*Dhalūlun lā tuthīru al-arḍa wa lā tasqī al-ḥarth.* Al-Jalālayn gives the grammar and the sense:

*He said, "He says, she shall be a cow not broken — not subdued for labour — that is, to plough the earth, churning its soil for sowing; tuthīru al-arḍ, the clause describes the word dhalūl and constitutes part of the negation; or to water the tillage, that is, the land prepared for sowing; one safe from faults and the effects of toil; with no blemish of a colour other than her own on her."*

Tanwīr al-Miqbās: *Surely she is a cow unyoked — unfettered; she plougheth not the soil — she is not subjugated for the ploughing of the soil, nor watereth the tilth — nor for carrying water to irrigate it.*

A working cow has marks: a yoke callus, worn hooves, muscle from the plough. This one has none. It has never worked.

**Whole and without blemish.**

*Musallamatun lā shiyata fīhā.* Tanwīr al-Miqbās: *whole — free from any blemish — and without mark — spots or flecks of white.*

Al-Mukhtaṣar: *she had no faults, and no marks of a different colour other than her yellow.*

Perfect yellow, unworked, unmarked. The description that began as *slaughter a cow* has become the most specific animal in the Qurʾān.

**"Now you have come with the truth."**

*Al-āna jiʾta bi-l-ḥaqq.* Al-Jalālayn glosses it: *They said, "Now you have brought the truth" — that is, now you have explained it clearly.*

Tanwīr al-Miqbās: *now we know the cow's right description.*

Al-Mukhtaṣar: *They then replied that now he had brought them a detailed description, correctly identifying the cow.*

*Now.* After three questions. The implication is that the earlier answers had not been the truth — which is an extraordinary thing to say to a prophet about a revelation, and the verse records it without comment.

**Who owned it.**

Al-Jalālayn tells the story of the search, and it is the detail everyone remembers:

*They thus sought it out and found it with a boy very dutiful towards his mother, and they eventually purchased it for the equivalent of its weight in gold.*

*A boy very dutiful towards his mother.* The only cow in the region matching the description belonged to the one person whose piety explains why he had it — an unworked, unmarked, beautiful animal that nobody else would have kept idle.

Tanwīr al-Miqbās: *They looked for it and bought her in exchange for her weight in gold.*

Ibn Kathīr's version, from ʿUbaydah, gives the negotiation:

*They found the designated cow with a man, the only one who owned that cow. He said, "By Allah! I will only sell it for its skin's fill of gold." So they paid the cow's fill of its skin in gold.*

*Its skin's fill of gold.* Not its weight — enough gold to fill the hide. Al-Jalālayn's *weight in gold* and Ibn Kathīr's *skin's fill* are both recorded, and the second is the harsher bargain.

**They slaughtered it hesitantly.**

*Wa mā kādū yafʿalūn.* Al-Jalālayn: *and so they sacrificed her, even though they very nearly did not, on account of its excessive cost.*

Tanwīr al-Miqbās: *So they sacrificed her, though almost they did not — i.e. initially; as it is said, because the cow was hugely expensive.*

Al-Mukhtaṣar: *They sacrificed it, after almost not having done it, due to all their arguing and stubbornness.*

*Mā kādū* — they almost did not. The command was obeyed, and the verse records that it nearly was not.

**The ḥadīth that closes the story.**

Al-Jalālayn gives it in the form that has been quoted for a thousand years:

*In a ḥadīth it is stated that "Had they sacrificed any cow it would have sufficed them, but they made it difficult for themselves, and so God made it difficult for them."*

Ibn Kathīr states it from Ibn ʿAbbās and ʿUbaydah: *Had they slaughtered a cow, any cow, it would have been sufficient for them. Instead, they made the matter difficult, and this is why Allah made it even more difficult for them.*

Maʿārif: *The ḥadīth says that if these people had obeyed Allah's commandment without raising so many doubts and asking unnecessary questions, such strict condition would not have been imposed on them, and the sacrifice of any cow whatsoever would have been accepted.*

Three sources, one ḥadīth, one meaning. Any cow.

**And what the cow was for.**

Ibn Kathīr supplies the ending, which verse 73 will state:

*They paid the cow's fill of its skin in gold, slaughtered it and touched the dead man with a part of it. He stood up, and they asked him, "Who killed you?" He said, "That man," and pointed to his nephew. He died again, and his nephew was not allowed to inherit him. Thereafter, whoever committed murder for the purpose of gaining inheritance was not allowed to inherit.*

A ruling comes out of it. The nephew's motive was the inheritance, and the ruling that followed closed the loophole for everyone after him.

**Tazkīrul's reading of the whole passage.**

It draws the lesson the sūrah is teaching:

*They had to learn to interpret God's will in a straightforward manner and obey it immediately. This was another lesson that was taught under the pretext of this murder case: hair-splitting to define the exact scope of divine edicts will only make things difficult for everyone; additional conditions will only complicate the carrying out of what had originally been a simple commandment.*

*Under the pretext of this murder case.* A man was killed, a town nearly went to war, a prophet was accused of mockery, an orphan-keeping boy's cow was bought for its skin's weight in gold — and the lesson is about how to receive a command.

**Why this story names the sūrah.**

Two hundred and eighty-six verses. The cow appears in five of them. But those five contain the sūrah's whole method in miniature: a command given plainly, received as a joke, narrowed by three questions, made costly by the narrowing, obeyed at the last moment, and ending in a ruling that outlived the event.

*Slaughter a cow.* That was all it was. And it took five verses and a skin's fill of gold to get it done.

72.text:
*This is when a man was killed and you disputed who the killer was, but Allah revealed what you concealed.*

**The murder, stated at last.**

Verses 67 to 71 told the story of the cow without ever saying why a cow. Verse 72 goes back and gives the reason — and the sūrah's word order is worth noticing. The command came first. The explanation comes five verses later.

Al-Jalālayn flags the structure: *this is a parenthetical statement; the story begins here with "and when you killed a soul," and continues in the following [verse].*

**What the dispute was.**

Ibn Kathīr collects four glosses on *faddāraʾtum*:

*Al-Bukhārī said that "and disagreed among yourselves as to the crime" means, "Disputed." This is also the tafsīr of Mujāhid. ʿAṭāʾ al-Khurāsānī and aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk said, "Disputed about this matter." Also, Ibn Jurayj said that it means, some of them said, "You killed him," while the others said, "No, you killed him." This is also the tafsīr of ʿAbd ar-Raḥmān ibn Zayd ibn Aslam.*

Ibn Jurayj's version gives the shape of it: accusations flying in both directions, nobody conceding.

Al-Mukhtaṣar adds where it went: *They accused each other of it, each rejecting the accusation of having killed him, and accusing someone else, until they fought.*

*Until they fought.* This is verse 67's scene — the town arming itself by morning.

**Maʿārif supplies the missing piece.**

He explains why the dispute happened at all, and it is the detail that makes the verse indicting rather than merely descriptive:

*The murderer had his supporters who wanted to hide his crime, and hence began accusing different people.*

*His supporters.* Not a lone killer. A party with an interest in the outcome — which fits Ibn Kathīr's account from ʿUbaydah, where the killer was the sole heir.

Al-Mukhtaṣar closes the verse: *But Allah revealed what they were hiding about the murder of the innocent person.*

*The innocent person.* The only source to say so.

**Who the dead man was.**

Tanwīr al-Miqbās names him: *And remember when ye slew a man — ʿĀmil — and disagreed concerning it, concerning his murder.*

The same name that appeared in Tanwīr's gloss on verse 70, where "we will be guided" was read as *we may be led to the murder of ʿĀmil*. One report, carried through both verses.

**The grammar of concealment.**

Al-Jalālayn notes the word's form: *iddāraʾtum — the tāʾ of the root-form itdāraʾtum has been assimilated with the dāl.*

And Mujāhid's gloss on the verse's second half: *"But Allah brought forth that which you were taktumūn" means, "what you were hiding."*

*Taktumūn* — what you were concealing, deliberately, as a group. Not what you did not know. What you were hiding.

**Why this verse sits after the cow and not before it.**

The sūrah could have opened the story with the murder. It did not. It gave the command, the mockery, the three questions, the price — and only then said why.

The effect is that the reader spends five verses thinking the command is arbitrary. Then verse 72 reveals that a man was dead and a town was fighting.

Maʿārif's summary: *But Allah willed that the criminal should be brought to book, and appointed a miraculous way of identifying him.*

*Brought to book.* The cow was a legal instrument. That is what the whole passage has been about, and verse 72 is where it becomes visible.

73.text:
*So We instructed, "Strike the dead body with a piece of the cow." This is how easily Allah brings the dead to life, showing you His signs so that you may understand.*

**The verse the whole story was for.**

Five verses of negotiation over a cow, and this is what it was bought for.

**Strike him with a piece of it.**

Ibn Kathīr's reading is the most permissive, and it matters:

*"Strike him — the dead man — with a piece of it — the cow" — meaning, "any part of the cow will produce the miracle (if they struck the dead man with it)."*

Any part. The miracle was not in a specific organ.

Then he says something rare and important about how to read the Qurʾān:

*We were not told which part of the cow they used, as this matter does not benefit us either in matters of life or religion. Otherwise, Allah would have made it clear for us. Instead, Allah made this matter vague, so this is why we should leave it vague.*

*Allah made this matter vague, so we should leave it vague.* A principle of interpretation stated in one line: where the text is silent, the silence is deliberate.

**What the other sources say anyway.**

The commentators do not all follow that principle, and the reports differ:

Al-Jalālayn: *so when he was struck with its tongue or its tail, he came back to life.*

Tanwīr al-Miqbās: *with some of it — with an organ of the cow; and it is also said: with its tail or tongue.*

Tongue or tail. Two guesses, both recorded, neither settled — exactly as Ibn Kathīr predicted.

**What happened.**

Al-Jalālayn gives the fullest account:

*He came back to life and said, "So-and-so killed me," and after pointing out two of his cousins he died; the two killers were denied the inheritance and were later killed.*

*Two of his cousins.* Note the number — verse 67's account had one nephew. Al-Jalālayn has two cousins. Both reports stand in the tradition.

Ibn Kathīr supplies the verse's own reading of what happened next: *"Thus Allah brings the dead to life" means, "They struck him with it, and he came back to life."*

He then states the verse's purpose in the argument with its audience: *Allah made this incident proof against the Jews that the Resurrection shall occur, and ended their disputing and stubbornness over the dead person.*

*Ended their disputing.* Verse 72's word was *faddāraʾtum* — you disputed. Verse 73 says the dispute was closed. Not by argument, but by the dead man standing up.

Al-Mukhtaṣar gives the plain sequence: *They did this and he told them who had killed him.*

Tanwīr al-Miqbās: *Thus — just as He brought ʿĀmil back to life.*

**The legal consequence.**

Al-Jalālayn: *the two killers were denied the inheritance and were later killed.*

Ibn Kathīr, in his account at verse 71: *his nephew was not allowed to inherit him. Thereafter, whoever committed murder for the purpose of gaining inheritance was not allowed to inherit.*

A permanent ruling came out of a single case. The motive was the inheritance, and the law was changed so the motive would never work again.

**This is how Allah brings the dead to life.**

*Kadhālika yuḥyī Llāhu al-mawtā.* Ibn Kathīr states the verse's argument:

*"Thus Allah brings the dead to life" means, "They struck him with it, and he came back to life." This verse demonstrates Allah's ability in bringing the dead back to life. Allah made this incident proof against the Jews that the Resurrection shall occur, and ended their disputing and stubbornness over the dead person.*

Maʿārif makes the same point more sharply:

*This miraculous event is a manifestation of the omnipotence of Allah, and the Holy Qurʾān presents it as an argument against those who deny the Resurrection of the dead for the Last Judgment. Verse 73 says that this precedent should induce people to make use of their reason, and see that what has happened in a past instance can as easily happen in a future instance.*

*A past instance* and *a future instance*. The argument is not "God is powerful." It is "this already happened once, so the mechanism is demonstrated."

Al-Jalālayn gives the reasoning in its simplest form: *that you might reflect and realise that the One capable of reviving a single soul is also capable of reviving a multitude of souls, and then believe.*

Tazkīrul Qurʾān states it as the third lesson of the story: *life after death is no less a reality than life before death. Just as the dead corpse was revived, so every soul will be raised up in the Hereafter and given new life.*

**The five resurrections in this sūrah.**

Ibn Kathīr notes something easy to miss — that sūrah 2 contains five accounts of the dead being raised, and this is the second:

*Allah mentioned His bringing the dead back to life in five instances in sūrat al-Baqarah. First Allah said, "Then We raised you up after your death." He then mentioned the story about the cow. Allah also mentioned the story of those who escaped death in their land, while they were numbering in the thousands. He also mentioned the story of the Prophet...*

Five resurrections in one sūrah. The first was verse 56 — the seventy men. This is the second. The sūrah is building a case, not telling isolated stories.

**Why the cow was needed at all.**

Maʿārif raises the obvious objection and answers it, and the answer is the most interesting thing in his commentary on the passage:

*With regard to this event one may ask as to why Allah made the resurrection of the dead man depend upon his being touched with a part of flesh, when he had the power to bring the man back to life without the intervention of any such device; or, one may ask as to why the dead man should have been brought back to life, when the name of the murderer could have been revealed even otherwise.*

*In answer to this, we shall say that Allah is omnipotent, and does not act under any kind of compulsion, but that all His actions proceed from His all-embracing wisdom. Moreover, it is He alone who knows, and can know, the raison d'être of what He does. The Sharīʿah does not oblige us to discover the raison d'être of each and every divine act.*

He asks the question, does not dodge it, and then sets a limit on what can be answered. That is a more honest treatment than most commentaries give.

**The three lessons of the story.**

Tazkīrul Qurʾān counts them, and this verse carries the third:

*The third lesson in this instance was that life after death is no less a reality than life before death. Just as the dead corpse was revived, so every soul will be raised up in the Hereafter and given new life.*

The first two were the Sabbath-breakers and the hair-splitting over the cow. The third is the one this verse states outright, and it is the only one of the three that concerns everybody rather than the Israelites alone.

**So that you may understand.**

*Laʿallakum taʿqilūn.* Al-Mukhtaṣar: *Allah gives humanity clear signs of His power, to make them reflect and understand, and have true faith in Him.*

Tanwīr al-Miqbās: *so that ye may understand — in order that you may believe in resurrection after death.*

Three things, in order: signs, understanding, faith. Not signs and faith. Understanding sits between them.

**And verse 74.**

The dead man spoke. The killers heard him. They denied it anyway.

That is what the next verse is about.

74.text:
*Even then your hearts became hardened like a rock or even harder, for some rocks gush rivers; others split, spilling water; while others are humbled in awe of Allah. And Allah is never unaware of what you do.*

**The sūrah's central image.**

After the exodus, the sea, the manna, the mountain, the springs, the resurrection — this. Hearts harder than stone.

Ibn Kathīr frames it: *Allah criticized the Children of Israel because they witnessed the tremendous signs and the āyāt of Allah, including bringing the dead back to life, yet "then after that your hearts were hardened."*

*Even after that.* The verse opens with *thumma* — then, after all that.

**Harder than rock — and why.**

Al-Mukhtaṣar gives the reason for the comparison, and it is the sharpest gloss available:

*Their hearts became hard after these great lessons and incredible miracles, until they became like rocks, and even harder than rocks, because they never changed, whereas rocks change and transform.*

*Whereas rocks change.* The comparison is not about hardness. It is about capacity to change. Rocks do three things in this verse. Their hearts did none of them.

Tanwīr al-Miqbās: *your hearts were hardened — dry and barren — and became as rocks, or worse than rock, for hardness.*

**The three kinds of rock.**

Ibn Kathīr lists them, and Maʿārif sets them out as a numbered scheme:

*In contrasting the hearts of the Israelites with stones, the verse refers to three states of the latter: (1) Some stones give forth a great amount of water. (2) Others give forth only a small quantity. (3) Still others do not give forth water, but fall down from their place for fear of Allah.*

*Some rocks gush rivers.* The first kind produces abundantly.

*Others split, spilling water.* Al-Jalālayn notes the grammar: *others split — yashshaqqaq, the initial tāʾ of the root-form yatashaqqaq has been assimilated with the shīn — so that water issues from them.*

*Others are humbled in awe of Allah.* The third kind gives nothing visible at all, and falls.

Tanwīr al-Miqbās: *and indeed there are some which fall down — from the top of mountains to the bottom — for the fear of Allah, but your hearts are not moved by fear of Allah.*

**The hardest question in the verse.**

Maʿārif raises the one everybody thinks of, and answers it seriously:

*The first two of these states are a matter of everyday observation, but the third may be subject to doubt, for the ability to feel fear requires reason and sensibility, and the stones, as one supposes, do not possess these faculties.*

*But reason is not always a necessary requisite for the ability to feel fear — after all, animals do feel fear, even though they do not possess reason. Sensibility is, of course, necessary. But there is no rational argument which should deny sensibility to minerals. For sensibility depends on life, and the minerals may possibly possess a kind of subtle life which man may not be aware of.*

He then adds, with evident satisfaction: *In fact, scientists have recently discovered the signs of life and sensibility in minerals too.*

A nineteenth-century commentator using contemporary science to defend a verse about rocks falling in fear. Whatever one makes of the argument, he did not wave the difficulty away.

**Tazkīrul's three readings.**

Tazkīrul Qurʾān turns the three rocks into three kinds of person, and it is the most beautiful passage in the six sources on this verse:

*1. One sees in the mountains how streams flow over the rocks, finally to join together to form a river. This is symbolic of a certain type of human being: one in whose heart fear of God is lodged, like water in the bosom of a mountain. This fear of the Lord flows from his eyes in the form of tears, as streams flow down the crags of the hillside.*

*2. Some rocks seem to be nothing more than dry boulders; but when cracked, reveal huge pools of water beneath them — wells from which people quench their thirst. This is on a parallel with one who, at first sight, appears to be far from the Lord. But then he is struck by some calamity, which shakes his soul. With floods of tears in his eyes he hastens to turn towards God.*

*3. Sometimes one sees landslides on mountain sides, with great slabs of rock crashing down the slopes.*

Three responses to the same mountain: flow, break and pour, collapse. And the hearts in the verse do none of them.

Tazkīrul's diagnosis is the harshest in the passage:

*Those who seek to find loopholes in God's commandments become more and more insensitive. God is another name for the most supreme of beings. If man's faith is a living faith, belief in God shakes his soul so deeply that his verbosity is replaced by stunned silence.*

*Verbosity replaced by stunned silence.* That is the opposite of the three questions about the cow.

*But when the heart is hardened, people begin to manipulate the divine scriptures, for they are used to doing the same with human writings.*

Verse 75 is about exactly that.

**Al-Jalālayn on the hearts.**

*While your hearts are unmoved, unstirred and not humbled.*

Three negations for three kinds of rock. Each rock does something. The hearts do nothing.

**Allah is never unaware.**

Al-Jalālayn's gloss is the most precise: *And God is not heedless of what you do — but instead He gives you respite until your time comes.*

*Gives you respite.* Not unaware and not inactive — waiting.

Tanwīr al-Miqbās: *Allah is not unaware of — will not leave unpunished — what ye do of transgressions; and it is said the meaning is: what you hide of transgression.*

*What you hide.* The same word as verse 72's *taktumūn* — what you were concealing. The verse closes on concealment, which is where the murder began.

Al-Jalālayn also notes a variant: *taʿmalūna, "you do" — a variant reading has yaʿmalūna, "they do," indicating a shift to the third person address.*

The same shift as verse 59, where the verse stepped back from addressing them.

**Why the verse matters to the reader.**

Ibn Kathīr supplies the cross-reference that makes it universal, and it is directed at Muslims:

*So their hearts were like stones that never become soft. This is why Allah forbade the believers from imitating the Jews when He said: "Has not the time come for the hearts of those who believe to be affected by Allah's Reminder, and that which has been revealed of the truth, lest they become as those who received the Scripture before, and the term was prolonged for them and so their hearts were hardened? And many of them were fāsiqūn" (57:16).*

*Lest they become as those who received the Scripture before.* The warning is not to the Children of Israel. It is to whoever is reading.

Ibn ʿAbbās's account of the nephews denying the dead man's testimony is what earns the verse. They heard a murdered man name them. They said he was lying.

And their hearts, the verse says, were harder than the rock that gushes rivers.

75.text:
*Do you still expect them to be true to you, though a group of them would hear the word of Allah then knowingly corrupt it after understanding it?*

**The address turns to the believers.**

Verses 40 to 74 spoke to the Children of Israel. Verse 75 turns and speaks to somebody else — and every one of the six commentators notices the shift.

Ibn Kathīr: *"Do you covet," O believers, "that they will believe in your religion" — meaning, that these people would obey you? They are the deviant sect of Jews whose fathers witnessed the clear signs but their hearts became hard afterwards.*

Al-Jalālayn gives the grammar of the rebuke:

*Are you then so eager, O believers, that they — the Jews — should believe you, seeing there is a party of them, a group of their rabbis, that heard God's word in the Torah and then tampered with it, changing it, and that after they had comprehended it, after they had understood it, knowingly, knowing full well that they were indulging in mendacity.*

*The hamza at the beginning of the verb a-fa-taṭmaʿūna is an interrogative for rejection — in other words, "Do not be so eager, for they have disbelieved before."*

An interrogative that is not a question. The same construction as 2:44 and 2:61.

Tanwīr al-Miqbās addresses it to the Prophet directly: *do you hope, O Muhammad, that the Jews will believe in you?*

**Why the Muslims expected it.**

Tazkīrul Qurʾān gives the historical reason, and it explains why this verse had to be revealed:

*One of the reasons for the promptness with which the people of Madinah recognized the Prophet Muhammad, and believed in him, was that they had often heard from their Jewish neighbours of the coming of a final prophet. They had, therefore, been expecting his arrival. The Jews then were responsible for the Muslims' initial fervour for Islam.*

*The Jews were responsible for the Muslims' initial fervour.* The very people the verse warns about are the reason the believers were confident.

*It was only natural that the Muslims, in their turn, should hope that the Jews would unhesitatingly accept the prophethood of Muhammad. With every hope of a positive response, it was with sublime feelings that they called on the Jews to join them in their belief in the Prophet. How shocked the Muslims were, then, when they found that, contrary to their expectations, the Jews were not ready to accept their invitation.*

And then the cost of that shock:

*Their efforts had the opposite effect, for the Prophet's opponents took the opportunity to ask the Muslims, "How are you so sure about the prophethood of Muhammad? If he were truly a prophet, the Jews would have been the first to believe in him, for their knowledge of what is written in the scriptures is greater than yours."*

A real apologetic problem, created by the Jewish refusal. And Tazkīrul's answer:

*But acceptance of a truth is not dependent upon knowledge alone; one has also to be sincere.*

**What "the word of Allah" refers to.**

There are two identifications, and Maʿārif gives both:

*The "Word of Allah" mentioned in the verse refers to the Torah, which the Jews had "heard" from the prophets, and the distortion pertains to the changes made in the words themselves or in the sense or in both; or it refers to the words of Allah which the seventy men had heard directly on Mount Ṭūr (Sinai), where they had gone to seek divine confirmation of what Sayyidunā Mūsā had been telling, and the distortion pertains to their declaration before their people that Allah had promised to forgive them if they could not act upon certain commandments.*

The second reading connects this verse straight back to verse 63 — the seventy men who went to hear God attest the Torah, came back, and added a permission He had not given. Maʿārif is the only commentator to make that link.

Tanwīr al-Miqbās takes the second reading: *when a party of them — the seventy men who were with Mūsā — used to listen to the Word of Allah, used to listen to Mūsā reciting the Word of Allah, then used to change it.*

**Who the group was.**

Al-Jalālayn: *a group of their rabbis.*

Mujāhid, recorded by Ibn Kathīr: *"Those who used to alter it and conceal its truths; they were their scholars."*

Al-Mukhtaṣar: *A group of their scholars heard the word of Allah, revealed to them in the Torah, and then changed its words and meanings after they had understood what it really meant; and they did this fully aware of the seriousness of the crime.*

Qatādah, via Ibn Kathīr: *"They are the Jews who used to hear Allah's Words and then alter them after they understood and comprehended them."*

Scholars. Not the masses. The people whose job was transmission.

**After they understood it, knowingly.**

Two phrases, and the second is what makes the verse severe.

Ibn Kathīr: *"after they understood it" — they understood well, yet they used to defy the truth — "knowingly," being fully aware of their erroneous interpretations and corruption.*

Then he gives the parallel verse that fixes the meaning: *"So, because of their violation of their covenant, We cursed them and made their hearts grow hard. They change the words from their right places" (5:13).*

*They change the words from their right places.* Not deleting them. Moving them. The same charge as verse 59, where one word became another.

Al-Mukhtaṣar: *they did this fully aware of the seriousness of the crime.*

**Maʿārif on why this is addressed to the Muslims.**

He explains the pastoral purpose, and it is the gentlest reading in the six sources:

*The Muslims used to take great pains in trying to make the Jews accept Islam. Having recounted so many stories of the perversity of the Jews, the Holy Qurʾān points out to the Muslims that they cannot expect such a people to be sensible, and asks them not to worry much about them. For, some of the Jews have been committing an even more heinous sin — they used to change and distort the Word of Allah in spite of knowing the ignominy of such a deed.*

*Asks them not to worry much about them.* After thirty-five verses of indictment, the point is not condemnation. It is that the Muslims should stop exhausting themselves.

**And the verse that makes it uncomfortable.**

Maʿārif then says something that lands on the reader as much as on the addressees:

*The Jews who were the contemporaries of the Holy Prophet may not have themselves been involved in some of these transgressions, but since they did not abhor the misdeeds of their forefathers, they are to be considered as their counterparts.*

*Since they did not abhor the misdeeds of their forefathers.* Not for doing it. For approving of it after the fact.

That is the same standard verse 2:208-209 will apply to everyone, and it is the reason the whole address to the Children of Israel is being delivered to an audience in Madinah.

**The verse's place.**

Verse 74 said their hearts were harder than rock. Verse 75 says what hardened hearts do: they edit revelation.

Tazkīrul's line covers both: *when the heart is hardened, people begin to manipulate the divine scriptures, for they are used to doing the same with human writings.*

And the sūrah has now named the sequence completely. Mockery, questions, cost, denial, hardness, distortion. Verse 76 shows what it looks like in conversation.

76.text:
*When they meet the believers they say, "We believe." But in private they say to each other, "Will you disclose to the believers the knowledge Allah has revealed to you, so that they may use it against you before your Lord? Do you not understand?"*

**The verse that describes a private conversation.**

The Qurʾān records what a group said when nobody else was in the room — and the reason it can is stated two verses later.

**What they said in public.**

Al-Jalālayn: *And when they — the hypocrites from among the Jews — meet those who believe, they say, "We believe" — that Muhammad is a prophet, and that he is the one of whom we have been given good tidings in our Book.*

Tanwīr al-Miqbās names the believers: *And when they fall with those who believe — Abū Bakr and his Companions — they say: We believe in your Prophet, and his description and traits are mentioned in our Book.*

Al-Mukhtaṣar: *some of them met some believers and acknowledged the truth of the Prophet Muhammad, and the correctness of his message, as the Torah witnessed to it.*

Not a vague profession. A specific claim, drawn from their own scripture, made to the people it would convince most.

**What they said in private.**

Al-Jalālayn identifies who is speaking to whom, and it is not the hypocrites correcting themselves:

*But when they go in private one to another, they — their leaders, the ones not involved in the hypocrisy — say to those hypocrites: "Do you speak to them — the believers — of what God has disclosed to you, that is, what He has made known to you of Muhammad's description in the Torah, so that they may thereby dispute with you before your Lord in the Hereafter, and hold the proof against you for not following him despite your knowledge of his sincerity? Have you no understanding?" of the fact that they will contend with you if you speak to them in this way? So beware.*

The leaders are rebuking the hypocrites — not for lying, but for leaking. The hypocrisy is fine. The information is the problem.

Tanwīr al-Miqbās frames it as class: *it is also said that the reference here is to the lowly from among the people of the Book... when these lowly people return to their leaders, the leaders say to the lowly: "Prate ye to them of that which Allah hath disclosed to you about that which Allah has shown you regarding the description and traits of Muhammad in your Book."*

*Prate.* The word carries contempt. The leaders are annoyed with their own people for talking too much.

**The argument they were afraid of.**

Al-Jalālayn spells it out: *so that they may dispute with you before your Lord in the Hereafter, and hold the proof against you for not following him despite your knowledge of his sincerity.*

*Despite your knowledge of his sincerity.* The fear is not that the Muslims would learn something new. It is that they would learn that the Jews had always known.

Al-Jalālayn also notes a grammatical subtlety in the verse: *the lām of li-yuḥājjūkum, "that they may dispute with you," is the lām of "becoming."*

Not purpose. Consequence. They are not saying the Muslims intend to argue — they are saying the argument will inevitably follow.

**Maʿārif's account of how it worked in Madinah.**

He gives the social mechanics, and it is the clearest description in the six sources:

*Some of the Jews, seeing the growing power of the Muslims in Madinah and around it, pretended to have accepted Islam. In order to assure the Muslims of their sincerity and to win their favour, these hypocrites would now and then disclose to them that the Torah itself had given out the good tidings of the coming of the Holy Prophet and mentioned the Holy Qurʾān.*

*Seeing the growing power of the Muslims.* The motive is political, and Maʿārif says so plainly.

*But when they met other Jews who openly declared their adherence to Judaism, they would admit that they were only trying to deceive the Muslims, and were otherwise quite loyal to their own faith. On such occasions, those of the other group used to reprimand them for revealing to the Muslims what they themselves were trying to keep concealed, for a knowledge of the relevant verses of the Torah could be very useful for the Muslims in order to defeat the Jews in their argument.*

So: one group feigns belief to gain favour. The other group is angry — not at the feigning, but at the disclosure. Both groups agree the Torah predicts Muhammad. Neither will say so.

**Do you not understand?**

The verse ends with the leaders' contempt for their own people's intelligence.

Al-Jalālayn: *Have you no understanding? So beware.*

Tanwīr al-Miqbās: *Have ye then no sense? — do you not have any common sense?*

Al-Mukhtaṣar: *when they were alone with one another they blamed each other because of these acknowledgments, saying that the Muslims might use them as proof that they recognised the truth of Muhammad's prophethood.*

**Why this verse is here.**

Verse 75 said a group heard the word of Allah and corrupted it after understanding it. Verse 76 shows the same thing in operation — not in a text, but in a conversation.

The knowledge was intact. The Torah still said what it said. What had changed was what they were willing to say out loud, and to whom.

Ibn Kathīr's frame for verses 75 to 77 is a single heading: *There was little hope that the Jews who lived during the time of the Prophet could have believed.*

**And the verse that follows.**

Verse 77 answers the premise of the whole private conversation. They were managing information — deciding what to disclose, to whom, and with what consequence.

The next verse says Allah knows what they conceal and what they reveal.

Which is the same word the sūrah has used throughout: *taktumūn* at verse 72, *what you hide* at verse 74. Concealment is the thread running from the murder to the whispered conversation in Madinah.

And verse 76 is the sūrah's evidence that it knows about the whispers too.
